The status of **religious freedom in Europe** varies from country to country. [States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_(polity) "State (polity)") can differ based on whether or not they guarantee [equal treatment under law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equality_under_law "Equality under law") for followers of different religions, whether they establish a [state religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_religion "State religion") (and the legal implications that this has for both practitioners and non-practitioners), the extent to which religious organizations operating within the country are policed, and the extent to which [religious law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_law "Religious law") is used as a basis for the country's legal code.

There are further discrepancies between some countries' self-proclaimed stances of religious freedom in law and the actual practice of authority bodies within those countries: a country's establishment of religious equality in their [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution "Constitution") or [laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law") does not necessarily translate into freedom of practice for residents of the country. Additionally, similar practices (such as having religious organizations register with the government) can have different consequences depending on other [sociopolitical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociopolitical "Sociopolitical") circumstances specific to the countries in question.  Virtually every country in Europe legally establishes the freedom of religion for people living in the country, and most also have anti-discrimination laws that specifically highlight religious freedom. However, enforcement of these laws is not always consistent, and several countries routinely fail to implement these laws at a local level. A few countries in Europe continue to have state religions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu81-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu84-2) Most countries in the former [Eastern bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_bloc "Eastern bloc") have government programs for the restitution of religious property confiscated by previous [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist "Socialist") governments.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu9-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu82-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu02-5) Many countries in Europe also provide government funding or other privileges for registered religious groups.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu78-6)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu81-1)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu0-7) Several countries have [animal slaughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter "Animal slaughter") laws that effectively ban butchers from making [kosher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kosher "Kosher") and [halal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halal "Halal") meat, and a smaller proportion ban non-medical circumcision, generally on the grounds of [animal rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_rights "Animal rights") and [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") respectively. In most cases, religious individuals that need to observe these practices are able to import meat and go to other countries to have circumcisions performed without interference from their government.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu7-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:slov-10)

Religious tolerance in general society varies across Europe. While some countries have a high degree of religious tolerance,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu0-7) others have significant levels of [Anti-Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobia "Islamophobia") and [anti-Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism "Antisemitism") sentiments in the general populace,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022BEL-11) as well as discrimination against [Jehovah's Witnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah's_Witnesses "Jehovah's Witnesses"), at times resulting in religiously-motivated physical violence or vandalism. In a few countries, particularly in former [Yugoslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia "Yugoslavia") states, but also [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine"), there are hostilities between Christian denominations connected to disputes between Orthodox churches over religious jurisdictions and the control of holy sites.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu2-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:ukr1-13)

## Albania

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Albania")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Albania "Freedom of religion in Albania")

The [constitution of Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Albania "Constitution of Albania") provides for freedom of religion, and the government respects this right in practice. The government of [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania "Albania") provides financial support to the Catholic Church, the [Albanian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albanian_Orthodox_Church "Albanian Orthodox Church"), Sunni Muslims, and [Bektashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bektashism_and_folk_religion "Bektashism and folk religion") Sufi Muslims.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:74-14)

The government of Albania is in the process of returning property confiscated from religious organizations during the [People's Socialist Republic of Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Socialist_Republic_of_Albania "People's Socialist Republic of Albania") (1944-1991). As of 2017, religious organizations have not prioritized engaging with the bureaucratic processes implemented by the government for the return of such property, and thus it remains in the government's possession.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:74-14)

In May 2017 [United Nations Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion or Belief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Special_Rapporteur_on_Freedom_of_Religion_or_Belief "United Nations Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion or Belief")[Ahmed Shaheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_Shaheed "Ahmed Shaheed") completed his assessment of the state of religious freedom in the country and stated, “Albania is a model for interfaith harmony.”[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:74-14)

Public schools are secular, and the law prohibits religious instruction in them. Private schools may offer religious instruction.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:74-14)

In 2023, Albania scored 4 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-15)

## Andorra

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Andorra")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Andorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Andorra "Freedom of religion in Andorra")

The [constitution of Andorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Andorra "Constitution of Andorra") provides for freedom of religion, and the [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Andorra "Government of Andorra") generally respects this right in practice. There is no state religion; however, the constitution acknowledges a special relationship with the Roman Catholic Church, which receives some privileges not available to other religious groups, such as salaries and expedited citizenship for clergy.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:75-16)

One of the two [Co-Princes of Andorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-Princes_of_Andorra "Co-Princes of Andorra") is the [Bishop of Urgell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Urgell "Bishop of Urgell"), in whose [diocese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese "Diocese")[Andorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andorra "Andorra") is located (the other is the [President of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France "President of France")).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:75-16)

Muslim and Jewish communities in Andorra (populations 800-2000 and 100 respectively) have been requesting that local municipalities allocate land for Muslim and Jewish cemeteries, in order for them to be able to bury people according to their ritual customs. As of 2017, no municipality has accepted these requests, although non-Christians are allowed to use existing cemeteries. The Muslim and Jewish communities continue to use cemeteries in [Toulouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse "Toulouse"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") in order to be able to follow their religious customs.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:75-16)

There are no mosques in Andorra, although there are two prayer rooms that are used by the Muslim community.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:75-16)

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-17)

## Austria

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Austria")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Austria "Freedom of religion in Austria")

Austria guarantees freedom of religion through various constitutional provisions and through membership in various international agreements. In Austria, these instruments are deemed to allow any religious group to worship freely in public and in private, to proselytize, and to prohibit discrimination against individuals because of their religious allegiances or beliefs. However, part of the Austrian constitutional framework is a system of cooperation between the government and recognized religious communities. The latter are granted preferential status by being entitled to benefits such as a tax-exempt status and public funding of religious education.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-OSCE-18)

Currently, Austria recognizes twelve religions. In addition to various Christian denominations including Jehovah's Witnesses, these include Judaism, Buddhism, and Islam. To date, Austria has not granted full recognition to several newer and allegedly controversial religions such as the Church of Scientology. Some newer religious groups, however, have applied under the 1998 Act and thereby attained the preliminary status of communities of believers.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-OSCE-18)

In October 2017, Austria passed a law banning the covering of one's face in public, which has been criticized as [Islamophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobia "Islamophobia") and a "criminalization of Muslim women" by various experts due to its effectively banning the usage of [burqas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burqa "Burqa") and other similar clothing.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Tahhan-21) There have been reports of [antisemitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism "Antisemitism"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-22) and [fascist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism") sympathizers with connections to the [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") have held elected office as recently as 2008.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-23)

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-24)

## Belarus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Belarus")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Belarus "Freedom of religion in Belarus")

The Constitution of Belarus provides for freedom of religion. However, the government restricts religious freedom in accordance with the provisions of a 2002 law on religion and a 2003 concordat with the [Belarusian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarusian_Orthodox_Church "Belarusian Orthodox Church") (BOC), a branch of the [Russian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox_Church "Russian Orthodox Church") (ROC) and the only officially recognized Orthodox denomination. Although there is no state religion, the concordat grants the BOC privileged status.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022BEL-11)

Foreign missionaries, clergy, and humanitarian workers affiliated with churches faced delays with visa applications which impacted their work.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022BEL-11)

Belarus is the only country in Europe to have jailed a newspaper editor for publishing the [Danish cartoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_cartoons "Danish cartoons") of the Islamic [Prophet Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet_Muhammad "Prophet Muhammad"). On January 18, 2008, [Alexander Sdvizhkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Sdvizhkov "Alexander Sdvizhkov") was jailed for three years for 'incitement of religious hatred'.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-25)

In 2023, Freedom House rated Belarus’ religious freedom as 1 out of 4.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-26)

## Belgium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Belgium")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Belgium "Freedom of religion in Belgium")

The [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Belgium "Constitution of Belgium") guarantees freedom of religion in [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), and the law prohibits discrimination based on religious orientation. There are, however, various laws prohibiting the operation of Muslim and Jewish religious slaughterhouses on animal cruelty grounds, as well as bans on Muslim veils and headscarves. Additionally, there have been several reports of [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism "Antisemitism") and [anti-Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Muslim_bigotry "Anti-Muslim bigotry") incidents, including hate speech, discrimination, and violence.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

### Legal framework

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legal framework")]

Belgian law states no individual may be barred from religious ceremonies or from observing religious days of rest, and bars the state from interfering in the appointment of religious clergy or blocking the publication of religious documents. It obligates the state to pay the salaries and pensions of religious clergy that are certified by the official organizations of recognized religions and employed in recognized houses of worship. Unrecognized groups do not receive government subsidies but may worship freely and openly. The law prohibits discrimination based on religious or philosophical (e.g., nonconfessional) orientation. Federal law prohibits public statements inciting religious hatred, including Holocaust denial.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

In 2017, [Wallonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallonia "Wallonia") and [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") regional governments passed laws, scheduled to take effect in 2019, banning the ritual slaughter of animals without prior stunning, effectively outlawing [kosher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashrut "Kashrut") and [halal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halal "Halal") practices.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

In the continuing aftermath of [2016 terrorist attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Brussels_bombings "2016 Brussels bombings"), the government extended its stated efforts to curb radical Islam, particularly following the release of a government report stating [Wahhabism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wahhabism "Wahhabism") constituted a threat to the practice of moderate Islam in the country.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

The government maintains a ban on Muslim women wearing headscarves in public sector jobs, and full-face veils (_[niqab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niq%C4%81b "Niqāb")_) are banned in public.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

### Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Education")]

The constitution requires teaching in public schools to be neutral with respect to religious belief. All public schools offer mandatory religious instruction or, alternatively, "moral" instruction (which is oriented towards citizenship and moral values), although parents in schools in Flanders may have their children opt out of such courses. A constitutional court ruling in 2015 allows [francophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francophone "Francophone") community parents to opt out of primary school religion and ethics classes for their children, pursuant to the court's finding those classes not to be "objective, critical, and pluralistic."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

Schools provide teachers for each of the recognized religious groups, as well as for secular humanism, according to the student's preference.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

### Societal attitudes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Societal attitudes")]

Unia, an anti-discrimination non-profit organization, reported it recorded 365 complaints of online hate speech in 2016 compared with 333 in 2015 (10 percent increase), with antisemitic and anti-Muslim hate speech representing the vast majority of cases. Unia reported an increase in antisemitic acts and threats from 57 in 2015 to 109 in 2016, the most recent year for which data were available.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

Unia reported there were 88 complaints of workplace discrimination based on religion in 2016, the latest year for which data were available, compared with 46 in 2015. Most of these complaints involved reports of discrimination against Muslims, especially against Muslim women for wearing headscarves.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

Jewish groups complained that Unia did not take antisemitism as seriously as other forms of discrimination. some Jewish leaders said there was a proliferation of online comments posted ostensibly as criticisms of the Israeli government but contained anti-Semitic elements such as rhetoric conflating Jews with Israeli government policy or blaming Jews for Israel's actions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

In September 2017 in Antwerp, a Belgian convert to Islam verbally and physically attacked a Jewish man.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

At least 100 young Muslim and Jewish leaders from around Europe came together in Brussels for a "Joint Day of Action against Anti-Semitism and Anti-Muslim Hatred and Discrimination," organized by the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe Office of Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and EU bodies on May 30. European Muslim and Jewish participants raised concerns about what they characterized as the stark rise of antisemitism and anti-Muslim sentiment in European societies, primarily fueled by political campaign rhetoric.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:76-8)

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-27)

## Bosnia and Herzegovina

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Bosnia and Herzegovina")]

See also: [Religion in Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Religion in Bosnia and Herzegovina")

The [constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), as well as the constitutions of its two constituent entities, [Republika Srpska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Republika_Srpska "Constitution of Republika Srpska") and the [Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), provide for freedom of religious thought and practice, prohibit religious discrimination, and allow registered religious organizations to operate freely.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28) Religion and ethnicity are closely linked in [Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Bosnia and Herzegovina"), and tensions between ethnic groups result in discriminatory practices as well as vandalism against religious sites.

### Legal framework

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Legal framework")]

A provision in the state constitution establishes representation quotas in government for the three main ethnoreligious groups in [Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Bosnia and Herzegovina"), [Bosniaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosniaks "Bosniaks") (predominantly Muslim, 51% of the population), [Serbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbs "Serbs") (predominantly [Serbian Orthodox Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbian_Orthodox_Christian "Serbian Orthodox Christian"), 31% of the population), and [Croats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croats "Croats") (predominantly Catholic, 15% of the population). As a consequence of these quotas, individuals belonging to religious minorities who are not members of the aforementioned ethnic groups cannot hold government office. According to a 2013 government census, 3% of the country's population belongs to minority religions.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

In addition to Islam, Catholicism, and Serbian Orthodox Christianity, [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism") is recognized as a "traditional religion" of Bosnia and Herzegovina and is automatically recognized by the government. Other religious groups may register with the government provided that they have at least 300 adult citizen members, subject to approval by the [Ministry of Justice.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Justice_(Bosnia_and_Herzegovina) "Ministry of Justice (Bosnia and Herzegovina)")[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

The state recognizes the [Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Community_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina") as the sole supreme institutional religious authority for all Muslims, including immigrants and refugees, as well as for Bosniaks and other Muslim nationals living outside the country who accept the Islamic Community's authority. According to the law, no Islamic group may register with the Ministry of Justice or open a mosque without the permission of the Islamic Community. Some unregistered groups practice Islam independently of the Islamic Community. Such groups are predominantly [Salafi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salafi_movement "Salafi movement") in theological orientation.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

### Government practices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Government practices")]

Observers reported government authorities were not enforcing the 2015 decision by the [High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Judicial_and_Prosecutorial_Council "High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council") prohibiting employees of judicial institutions from wearing any form of “religious insignia” at work, including headscarves.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

According to officials of minority religious groups, local authorities discriminate against them with regard to the use of religious property and issuance of permits for new religious properties. [Drvar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drvar "Drvar") municipal authorities refused construction permits for a new Catholic church, despite repeated requests from the local Catholic priest, the [Banja Luka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banja_Luka "Banja Luka") Catholic Diocese, and representatives from the [Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_for_Security_and_Co-operation_in_Europe "Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe"), which became directly engaged on the issue. Municipal authorities also continued to refuse to return any of the Catholic Church's nationalized properties, according to Church officials in Banja Luka.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

According to Catholic, Orthodox, and Jewish minorities, as well as Bosniak Muslims returning to a predominantly ethnic Serbian town, government authorities selectively enforced their rights, especially for refugees returning to their original communities pursuant to the [Dayton Peace Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dayton_Peace_Agreement "Dayton Peace Agreement"). Leaders of religious minority communities, particularly in [Canton 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_10 "Canton 10") in the western part of the Federation and several municipalities in eastern Republika Srpska, reported the failure of authorities to provide government services and protections to minorities, including access to health care, pensions, other social benefits, and the transfer of student records between districts. The leaders also said discrimination by local authorities continued when it came to providing police protection and investigating threats of violence, harassment, and vandalism. Because religion and ethnicity often are closely linked, it was difficult to categorize many actions as solely based on religious identity.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

NGOs, academics, and government agencies reported the continued association of each of the country's major political parties with the religion practiced by the dominant ethnic group among its membership. The biggest ethnic Bosniak parties continued to align with the Islamic Community, the biggest ethnic Croat parties with the Catholic Church, and the two largest ethnic Serb parties with the Serbian Orthodox Church.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

### Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Education")]

The law affirms the right of every citizen to religious education. The law calls for a representative of each of the officially registered religious communities to be responsible for teaching religious studies in all public and private pre-, primary, and secondary schools and universities. Children from minority religious groups are entitled to religious education only when there are 18 or more students from that religious group in one class. Religious communities select and train their respective religious education teachers. These individuals are employees of the schools where they teach, but they receive accreditation from the religious body governing the curriculum.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

Secondary students who do not wish to attend the religion class have the right to opt out if their school offers a class in ethics as an alternative, which many schools do. Parents of primary school students may request their child be exempted from religion class.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

According to nongovernmental organizations, provisions of the law regarding the religious education of returnee children remained unimplemented, particularly in segregated school systems, often at the behest of senior government authorities seeking to obstruct the process. Parents of more than 500 Bosniak children, who returned to their prewar homes in several Republika Srpska communities, continued to [boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycott "Boycott") public schools for a fifth year, choosing instead to send their children to alternative schools organized on the premises of the Islamic Community's administrative building and supported by the [Federation Ministry of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Education_(Federation_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ministry of Education (Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina) (page does not exist)"). Academic and NGO representatives reported continued social pressure on students from both majority and minority religious communities to attend instruction in their respective religions.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

### Societal attitudes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Societal attitudes")]

In October 2016 the Bosniak-dominated [Sarajevo Canton Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarajevo_Canton_Assembly "Sarajevo Canton Assembly") renamed a street and an elementary school after [Mustafa Busuladzic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustafa_Busulad%C5%BEi%C4%87 "Mustafa Busuladžić"), a World War II-era antisemite who glorified [Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler"). The president of the [Jewish Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarajevo_Jewish_Community?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sarajevo Jewish Community (page does not exist)") strongly condemned the act. Proponents claimed Busuladzic was not an antisemite despite his public support for the fascist [Ustashe Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ustashe "Ustashe").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

#### Religious violence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Religious violence")]

While the [Interreligious Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interreligious_Council_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Interreligious Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina") as of 2017 had registered nearly 200 incidences of violence against religious officials and sites since 2010, police identified the perpetrators in only 55 cases and courts prosecuted only 23 cases. According to the Interreligious Council, this low rate of prosecution reflects an ignorance about [hate crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_crime "Hate crime") and a tendency to deflect criticism of religious intolerance.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

Incidents of vandalism against the religious sites of all of the three primary religions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as against Jewish religious sites and property belonging to the Interreligious Council.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:77-28)

In 2023, the country scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-29)

## Bulgaria

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Bulgaria")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Bulgaria "Freedom of religion in Bulgaria")

The constitution of Bulgaria provides for freedom of religion, and other laws and policies contributed to the generally free practice of religion. However, the constitution designates Eastern Orthodox Christianity as the "traditional" religion, exempting it from having to register in court as required for all other religious groups.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022BULG-30)

In 2022, there were reports of societal abuses or discrimination based on religious affiliation, belief, or practice; in particular, there was an increasing number of antisemitic hate speech and graffiti, as well as vandalism against mosques and attacks on Jehovah's Witnesses.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022BULG-30)

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom;[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-31)

## Croatia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Croatia")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Croatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Croatia "Freedom of religion in Croatia")

The Constitution of [Croatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia "Croatia") provides for freedom of religion.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022CRO-32)

The [Catholic Church in Croatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_Croatia "Catholic Church in Croatia") receives state financial support and other benefits established in [concordats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concordat "Concordat") between the Government and the [Vatican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_See "Holy See"). The concordats and other government agreements with non-Catholic religious communities allow state financing for some salaries and pensions for religious officials through government-managed pension and health funds.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-countryreports_croatia-33)

The [Serbian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbian_Orthodox_Church "Serbian Orthodox Church") reports some difficulties in legal restitution regarding properties seized by the Yugoslav authorities.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022CRO-32)

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-34)

## Czech Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Czech Republic")]

Main article: [Religion in the Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_the_Czech_Republic "Religion in the Czech Republic")

Articles 15 and 16 of the [Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_Fundamental_Rights_and_Freedoms "Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms") (part of the constitutional system of the [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic")) include following statements: "The freedom of thought, conscience, and religious conviction is guaranteed. Everyone has the right to change her religion or faith or to have no religious conviction." and "Everyone has the right freely to manifest her religion or faith, either alone or in community with others, in private or public, through worship, teaching, practice, or observance."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-35)

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-36)

## Denmark

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Denmark")]

Main article: [Religion in Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Denmark "Religion in Denmark")

[![Image 5: Wikisource logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/40px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg)

English [Wikisource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikisource "Wikisource") has original text related to this article: 

**[Constitutional Act of Denmark, 5 June 1953](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/en:Constitutional%20Act%20of%20Denmark,%205%20June%201953 "s:en:Constitutional Act of Denmark, 5 June 1953")**

[Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark "Denmark") has [freedom of worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_worship "Freedom of worship"),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-37) however the [Church of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Denmark "Church of Denmark") does hold certain privileges. According to the [Constitution of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Denmark "Constitution of Denmark"), the [Evangelical Lutheran Church in Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Lutheran_Church_in_Denmark "Evangelical Lutheran Church in Denmark") is the [state church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_church "State church") of Denmark and receives some subsidies from the government.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-38) The constitution also mandates that the Danish [monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarch "Monarch") must be a member of the state church.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-39)

[Anti-Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobia "Islamophobia") organizations such as [Pegida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegida "Pegida") have organized demonstrations in Denmark in the 21st century, at times met by counter-protests.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-40) The [right-wing populist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-wing_populism "Right-wing populism")[Danish People's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_People's_Party "Danish People's Party") has at times self-described as an anti-Muslim party.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Berlingske_Media-41)

In 2023, the country was scored 4 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-42)

## Estonia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Estonia")]

Main article: [Religion in Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Estonia "Religion in Estonia")

Article 40 The Constitution of the [Republic of Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Estonia "Republic of Estonia") reads: "Everyone has freedom of conscience, religion and thought. Everyone may freely belong to churches and religious societies. There is no state church. Everyone has the freedom to exercise his or her religion, both alone and in community with others, in public or in private, unless this is detrimental to public order, health or morals."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-43)

In 2023, the country was scored 4 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-44)

## Finland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Finland")]

Main article: [Religion in Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Finland "Religion in Finland")

As the national churches of Finland, the [Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Lutheran_Church_of_Finland "Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland") and the [Finnish Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Orthodox_Church "Finnish Orthodox Church") have a status protected by law. The special legal position of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland is also codified in the constitution of Finland. Both churches have the right to levy an income tax on their members and every Finnish company as a part of Corporation Tax. The tax is collected by the state. The administration of the national churches is regulated by their respective church laws, which are drafted by the churches and enacted or rejected by the parliament. State universities, religiously non-aligned in themselves, provide the theological education that is required to be ordained as clergy of the national churches. The general direction has been to restrict and remove the privileges of the national churches, and as of 2004, in most other official business (such as officiating marriages) any registered religious community has a status comparable to that of the national churches.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-47)

In 2020, Juhani Pohjola, the head of the [Evangelical Lutheran Mission Diocese of Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Lutheran_Mission_Diocese_of_Finland "Evangelical Lutheran Mission Diocese of Finland") was investigated by the Prosecutor General of Finland and summoned to testify by the Helsinki Police Department[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-48) for being “suspected of being guilty of incitement to hatred against a group" for placing a small booklet[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-49) authored in 2004 on a website and distributing it through the church. The booklet summarized traditionalist doctrine on marriage and sexual matters; this included the statement that Leviticus 18:22, which instructs the reader to murder people who engage in homosexual behaviour, is the word of Christ.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-50) In 2022, Pohjola was prosecuted along with the article's author [Päivi Räsänen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A4ivi_R%C3%A4s%C3%A4nen "Päivi Räsänen"). Pohjola and Räsänen were found innocent by both the Helsinki district court and the Helsinki court of appeal;[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-52) consequently, the prosecutor applied to the Supreme Court of Finland for permission to appeal against the decision, which was given in 2024.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-53)

### Religion in schools

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Religion in schools")]

Teaching Christianity in schools continued after they became a part of municipal jurisdiction in 1866.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-54) Students, who were not members of either national church, gained the lawful right to be freed from such teaching with §8 of the Act of Religious Freedom of 1922 ([Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language"): _Uskonnonvapauslaki_, [Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Religionsfrihetslagen_). The legal guardian of the pupil had to apply for the pupil to be freed.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-55) Requirements for teacher competency for the teaching of religion and the corresponding subject for freed students "The history of religions and ethics" ([Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language"): _Uskontojen historia ja siveysoppi_, [Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Religionshistoria och etik_) have also varied.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-OPH-56)

Since 2003, world view related teaching is compulsory for all students in basic education (primary and secondary school). Each primary and secondary school municipality must arrange teaching in the religion that the majority of the students in the municipality are members of. Also, for every group of at least three students who belong to some other organized religion, teaching in their own religion must be arranged. For a group of at least three students within the municipality who do not belong to any organized religion, teaching in the subject "ethics"[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-57) ([Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_language "Finnish language"): _elämänkatsomustieto_, [Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _livsåskådningskunskap_), must be arranged. If there are too few students for a teaching group for the student's own religion to be arranged, the student (or as most such students are [minors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_(law) "Minor (law)"), their parents) can choose between joining the teaching group for the majority religion, requesting ethics education or arranging the teaching from their own religious organization.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-58) A teaching group for a minority religion or for ethics can be arranged for several schools together.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-OPH-56)

Current teacher education in Finland gives primary and secondary school teachers a basic competence to teach the national churches' religion, major [world religions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_religion "World religion") and ethics as school subjects. However, it is also noted that a teacher should not have to teach a particular religion if they object to it on the basis of conscience. Any conflicts between students' right to education and teachers' religious freedom should be solved on a case-by-case basis.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-OPH-56)

### Freedom of religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Freedom of religion")]

In 2023, the country was scored 4 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-59)

## France

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: France")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_France "Freedom of religion in France")

The [Constitution of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_France "Constitution of France") provides for the free exercise of religious worship. However, according to [Pew Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pew_Research_Center "Pew Research Center") in 2017, France has a high level of government restrictions on religion.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-60)

Since 1905, [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") has had a law requiring separation of church and state, prohibiting the state from recognizing or funding any religion. The [1905 law on secularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1905_law_on_secularity "1905 law on secularity") was highly controversial at the time, but today is held as a founding document of French secularism or _[laïcité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%C3%AFcit%C3%A9 "Laïcité")_. Some French politicians and communities have more recently questioned the law, arguing that, despite its explicit stance for [state secularism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_secularism "State secularism"), it _de facto_ favors traditional French religions, in particular the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"), at the expense of more recently established religions, such as [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_France "Islam in France"). The law provides for the transfer to the state of religious property built before 1905, with the local governments being expected to maintain the buildings at taxpayer's expense. Despite being state property, these buildings are available for religious use, provided that their use has been historically continuous.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Provisions-61) As most Roman Catholic churches in the country were built well before the enactment of the 1905, they are supported by the government.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-France24-62) With the exception of the historically anomalous Alsace-Lorraine,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Erlanger-63) followers of Islam and other religions more recently implanted in France instead have to build and maintain religious facilities at their own expense.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Morocco-64) In 2016, [President Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande") proposed a temporary ban on foreign funding for mosques[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Mulholland-65) and shut down at least 20 [mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mosques_in_France "List of mosques in France") found to be "preaching radical Islamic ideology".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Serhan-66)

In 2004, France passed a law banning the use of "conspicuous" religious symbols in public schools, including the [hijab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijab "Hijab").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-georgetown1-67) Many Muslims complained that the law infringed on their freedom of religion.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-68) Similarly the [Muslim Public Affairs Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Public_Affairs_Council "Muslim Public Affairs Council") called the ban "a major affront to freedom of religion", noting that many Muslims believe it is mandated by religious texts.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-69)[Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") and The [United States Commission on International Religious Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commission_on_International_Religious_Freedom "United States Commission on International Religious Freedom") expressed concern and disapproval at the law's passing.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-71)

On 14 September 2010, an act of parliament was passed resulting in the ban on the wearing of face-covering headgear, including [masks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask "Mask"), [helmets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmet "Helmet"), [balaclava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balaclava_(clothing) "Balaclava (clothing)"), [niqābs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niq%C4%81b "Niqāb") and other veils covering the face in public places, except under specified circumstances. The ban also applies to the [burqa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burqa "Burqa"), a full-body covering, if it covers the face.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-nyt20100713-72)

### Freedom of religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Freedom of religion")]

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-73) The bans on religious symbols and face coverings, like niqabs and burqas, in public places limit some aspects of religious freedom and expression.

## Georgia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Georgia")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Georgia "Freedom of religion in Georgia")

The [Constitution of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Georgia_(country) "Constitution of Georgia (country)") provides for freedom of religion, and the government generally respects this right in practice. However, some societal abuses of the freedom of religion have occurred. [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country) "Georgia (country)")_de facto_ lost control of the regions of [Abkhazia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abkhazia "Abkhazia") and [South Ossetia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Ossetia "South Ossetia") in 1993 and 1992 respectively, and does not exert control of these regions despite claiming them _de jure_.

Minority religious groups are viewed by some Georgians as a threat to Georgian national identity, cultural values, and the [Georgian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_Orthodox_Church "Georgian Orthodox Church"). Between 1999 and 2002, followers of a [defrocked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defrocked "Defrocked") former Georgian Orthodox priest, [Basil Mkalavishvili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Mkalavishvili "Basil Mkalavishvili"), attacked congregations of Jehovah's Witnesses and Baptists in Tbilisi.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-Violence_leaders_sentenced_2005-74) In 2011, eight members of Orthodox fundamentalist groups were sentenced to prison for breaking into a television station and assaulting participants on a talk show on religious freedom; however, after the [October 2012 parliamentary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_parliamentary_election,_2012 "Georgian parliamentary election, 2012") and the transition to a new government, these individuals were reclassified as "prisoners of conscience" and were freed as part of a general amnesty.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-IRL_20123-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-amnesty_2013-76) In November 2012, Muslims in a western Georgian community were prevented from gathering for prayer by Orthodox priests and townspeople; the local priest said that the local residents "would not allow any minarets and mass prayers in this village", and the police did not intervene.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-IRL_20123-75) During 2022, Jehovah's Witnesses reported nine incidences of threats and vandalism; in the same year, a man was sentenced to prison for threatened a Muslim leader during a service at a mosque.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022GEO-77)

In 2023, the country was scored 2 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-78)

### Abkhazia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Abkhazia")]

Main article: [Religion in Abkhazia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Abkhazia "Religion in Abkhazia")

The [Abkhazian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abkhazian_Orthodox_Church "Abkhazian Orthodox Church") operates outside the official [Eastern Orthodox ecclesiastical hierarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church_organization "Eastern Orthodox Church organization"), as all Eastern Orthodox churches recognise [Abkhazia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abkhazia "Abkhazia") as belonging to the jurisdiction of the [Georgian Orthodox church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_Orthodox_church "Georgian Orthodox church").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-80) The Georgian Orthodox Church lost effective control over the _Sukhumi-Abkhazian eparchy_ following the [1992-1993 war in Abkhazia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Abkhazia_(1992-1993) "War in Abkhazia (1992-1993)"), when ethnically Georgian priests had to flee Abkhazia. It maintains its structures in exile, where the current head is Archbishop Daniel.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-bible.ca-81) The Abkhazian Orthodox Church came into existence when the ethnically Abkhaz branch of the Sukhumi-Abkhazian Eparchy declared on 15 September 2009 that it no longer considered itself part of the [Georgian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_Orthodox_Church "Georgian Orthodox Church") and that it was re-establishing the [Catholicate of Abkhazia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholicate_of_Abkhazia "Catholicate of Abkhazia") disbanded in 1795.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-agov23092-82)

Jehovah's Witnesses are officially banned, but in the past some communities in some parts of Abkhazia have been able to establish working relationships with local authorities and have thereby been able to hold some meetings.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-IRL_20123-75)

### South Ossetia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: South Ossetia")]

The Georgian Orthodox Church has experienced interference from the _de facto_ government of [South Ossetia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Ossetia "South Ossetia"), which has banned Orthodox services in several ethnic Georgian villages; however, _de facto_ authorities have allowed them to conduct services there. Jehovah's Witnesses in "South Ossetia" are not officially recognized; however, they are able to assemble freely in [Akhalgori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akhalgori "Akhalgori").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022GEO-77)

## Germany

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Germany")]

Main article: [Freedom of religion in Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Germany "Freedom of religion in Germany")

The government prohibits religious discrimination and provides for freedom of faith and conscience and the practice of one’s religion.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022GER-83)

Today, church and state are "separate," but there is cooperation in many fields, most importantly in the social sector. Churches and religious communities, if they are large, stable and loyal to the constitution, can get special status from the state as a "corporation under public law" which allows the churches to levy taxes called Kirchensteuer (literally [church tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_tax "Church tax")) on their members. This revenue is collected by the state for a cost-covering fee. Payment of this tax is not voluntary for adherents of the respective religion who are otherwise obligated to pay taxes. Since one's religion is officially recorded, exemption from this tax is possible only through [leaving one's religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostasy "Apostasy"). Being a member of one's own religious tradition in Germany therefore requires monetary payment to the respective ecclesiastical body (and, indirectly, a small portion to the state).[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-84)

Religious instruction (for members of the respective religions) is an ordinary subject in public schools (in most states). It is organized by the state, but also under the supervision of the respective religious community. Teachers are educated at public universities, in departments that are nevertheless affiliated with a specific church (Protestant or Catholic) or with confessional Islam. Parents, or students 14 years old and above, can decide not to take those religion classes, but most federal states require classes in "ethics" or "philosophy" as replacements. A small but significant number of religious schools, which receive the majority of their funding (but never all of it) from the state, exist in most parts of the country; however nobody can be compelled to attend them. There was considerable public controversy when the Federal Constitutional Court declared a [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria") law requiring a [crucifix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifix "Crucifix") in every classroom to be unconstitutional in 1997; Bavaria replaced it with a law still demanding the same, unless parents file a formal protest with the state.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-85)

According to preliminary government figures, in 2022, there were over 2,500 antisemitic crimes reported;[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022GER-83) the government also reported that in 2021, there were 732 crimes targeting Muslims and over 100 anti-Christian crimes.

In 2023, the country was scored 4 out of 4 for religious freedom.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-86)

## Greece

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Greece")]

See also: [Religion in Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_Greece "Religion in Greece")

The [Constitution of Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Greece "Constitution of Greece") establishes the [Church of Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Greece "Church of Greece") as the "dominant" religion of Greece.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-87) Article 13 of the Constitution of Greece further guarantees the freedom of religion for all Greeks, although it also outlaws [proselytism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proselytism "Proselytism").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-88)

Orthodox, Catholic, and Jewish schools operate in the country as well as two Islamic religious schools in Thrace. Religious instruction is mandatory for all school pupils studying at grade three and higher, and students are taught the tenets of the Orthodox Christian faith (or, respectively, Islam, for the Muslim religious minority in Thrace) and general things about other religions and faiths.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-89) Typically, one hour per week (out of the 32-hour program of studies) is devoted to these lessons. However, students and parents can choose to opt out of religious instruction.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-US2022GREECE-90) The Lord's Prayer or another prayer is typically recited before lessons, once a day, but [school prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_prayer "School prayer") attendance is not mandatory.

An estimated 81.6 [[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-91) percent of the population identifies itself as Greek Orthodox. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne created an officially recognized "Muslim minority," which consists of an estimated 140,000 to 150,000 individuals (approximately 1.3 percent of the Greek population) residing in Thrace. The government supports the Orthodox Church financially by paying for clergy salaries, church maintenance, and exempting the Church from taxes on its property.

_Das Leben des Jesus_ (The Life of Jesus), a satire which portrays Jesus as an incense-addicted hippy, was banned in Greece in 2005 under a blasphemy statute, while its writer, [Gerhard Haderer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Haderer "Gerhard Haderer"), received a suspended six-month jail sentence. However, both the ban and sentence were repealed on appeal and the book has circulated freely since.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-92)

In 2006 an Athens court decreed the official recognition of the ancient Greek pantheon as a "known religion".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-94)

In 2023, the country was scored 3 out of 4 for religious freedom;[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-95) it was noted that the salaries and pensions of Orthodox clery are paid for by the state.

## Hungary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Hungary")]

See also: [Freedom of religion in Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Hungary "Freedom of religion in Hungary")

[Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary")'s laws establish the freedom of religion and belief, as well as prohibiting religious discrimination. Despite this, the government has selectively enforced some of these provisions, and significant portions of the country's population harbor anti-Jewish and anti-Muslim sentiments, with both communities facing harassment, discrimination, and violence.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu78-6) Government officials up to and including Prime Minister [Viktor Orbán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Orb%C3%A1n "Viktor Orbán") have made statements which have been criticized as anti-Muslim and anti-Jewish, although the government has also taken steps to support the Jewish community in Hungary.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu78-6)

### Legal framework

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Legal framework")]

The [Fundamental Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Hungary "Constitution of Hungary") of [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary"), the country's constitution, provides for freedom of conscience and religion, including freedom to choose or change religion or belief, and the freedom to manifest religion or belief through religious acts or ceremonies, or in any other way, in worshipping, practice, and observance. It prohibits religious discrimination as well as speech “aimed at violating the dignity” of any religious community.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu78-6)

The constitution's preamble states that “We recognize the role of Christianity” in preserving the nation and “value the various religious traditions” in the country. The constitution stipulates separation between religious communities and state and the autonomy of religious groups. According to the constitution, the state may, at the request of religious communities, cooperate with them on community goals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu78-6)

Implementing legislation provides for a dual system of religious communities, consisting of “incorporated churches” with which the state cooperates on community goals as outlined in the constitution, and “organizations engaged in religious activity”. Neither category is limited to Christian organizations. Religious organizations acquire incorporated church status through an application submitted to the [Ministry of Human Capacities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Human_Capacities_(Hungary)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ministry of Human Capacities (Hungary) (page does not exist)") and, if found eligible, by a subsequent two-thirds vote of parliament. However, despite an official 60 day deadline for the parliamentary decision, as of 2017 the [Parliament of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Hungary "Parliament of Hungary") has failed to vote on 14 applications previously approved by the MHC. Eligibility criteria evaluated by the MHC include the length of time that the religious organization has existed, the number of followers within Hungary, and the establishment of formal bylaws and religious practices. According to the government, more than 94 percent of citizens who reported a religious affiliation were affiliated with the four historical religious groups.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_Europe_by_country#cite_note-:eu78-6)

## Retired General Mark A. Milley

_20th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff_

![Image 2: Mark A. Milley](https://media.defense.gov/2023/Apr/04/2003192949/825/780/0/230216-D-LS763-0001.JPG)[Full image](https://media.defense.gov/2023/Apr/04/2003192949/-1/-1/0/230216-D-LS763-0001.JPG)

Retired General Mark A. Milley served as the 20th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the nation's highest-ranking military officer, and the principal military advisor to the President, Secretary of Defense, and National Security Council. He retired Sept. 29, 2023.

Prior to becoming Chairman on October 1, 2019, General Milley served as the 39th Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army.

A native of Massachusetts, General Milley graduated from Princeton University in 1980, where he received his commission from Army ROTC.

General Milley has had multiple command and staff positions in six divisions and a Special Forces Group throughout the last 44 years to include command of the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry, 2nd Infantry Division; the 2nd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division; Deputy Commanding General, 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault); Commanding General, 10th Mountain Division; Commanding General, III Corps; and Commanding General, U.S. Army Forces Command.

While serving as the Commanding General, III Corps, General Milley deployed as the Commanding General, International Security Assistance Force Joint Command and Deputy Commanding General, U.S. Forces Afghanistan. General Milley's joint assignments also include the Joint Staff operations directorate and as Military Assistant to the Secretary of Defense.

General Milley's operational deployments include the Multi-National Force and Observers Task Force, Sinai, Egypt; Operation JUST CAUSE, Panama; Operation UPHOLD DEMOCRACY, Haiti; Operation JOINT FORGE, Bosnia-Herzegovina; Operation IRAQI FREEDOM, Iraq; and three tours during Operation ENDURING FREEDOM, Afghanistan. GEN Milley also deployed to Colombia, Somalia and served two years on the DMZ in the Republic of Korea.

In addition to his bachelor's degree in political science from Princeton University, General Milley has a master's degree in international relations from Columbia University and one from the U.S. Naval War College in national security and strategic studies. He is also a graduate of the MIT Seminar XXI National Security Studies Program.

General Milley and his wife, Hollyanne, have been married for more than 38 years and have two children.

## Retired General Mark A. Milley

_20th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff_

![Image 2: Mark A. Milley](https://media.defense.gov/2023/Apr/04/2003192949/825/780/0/230216-D-LS763-0001.JPG)[Full image](https://media.defense.gov/2023/Apr/04/2003192949/-1/-1/0/230216-D-LS763-0001.JPG)

Retired General Mark A. Milley served as the 20th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the nation's highest-ranking military officer, and the principal military advisor to the President, Secretary of Defense, and National Security Council. He retired Sept. 29, 2023.

Prior to becoming Chairman on October 1, 2019, General Milley served as the 39th Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army.

A native of Massachusetts, General Milley graduated from Princeton University in 1980, where he received his commission from Army ROTC.

General Milley has had multiple command and staff positions in six divisions and a Special Forces Group throughout the last 44 years to include command of the 1st Battalion, 506th Infantry, 2nd Infantry Division; the 2nd Brigade Combat Team, 10th Mountain Division; Deputy Commanding General, 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault); Commanding General, 10th Mountain Division; Commanding General, III Corps; and Commanding General, U.S. Army Forces Command.

While serving as the Commanding General, III Corps, General Milley deployed as the Commanding General, International Security Assistance Force Joint Command and Deputy Commanding General, U.S. Forces Afghanistan. General Milley's joint assignments also include the Joint Staff operations directorate and as Military Assistant to the Secretary of Defense.

General Milley's operational deployments include the Multi-National Force and Observers Task Force, Sinai, Egypt; Operation JUST CAUSE, Panama; Operation UPHOLD DEMOCRACY, Haiti; Operation JOINT FORGE, Bosnia-Herzegovina; Operation IRAQI FREEDOM, Iraq; and three tours during Operation ENDURING FREEDOM, Afghanistan. GEN Milley also deployed to Colombia, Somalia and served two years on the DMZ in the Republic of Korea.

In addition to his bachelor's degree in political science from Princeton University, General Milley has a master's degree in international relations from Columbia University and one from the U.S. Naval War College in national security and strategic studies. He is also a graduate of the MIT Seminar XXI National Security Studies Program.

General Milley and his wife, Hollyanne, have been married for more than 38 years and have two children.

# New Army chief, looming force structure shakeups and new weapons: Army 2023 in review

The Army spent 2023 looking for ways to refill its weapon stockpiles, preparing for future conflicts and welcoming a new chief.

By [Ashley Roque](https://breakingdefense.com/author/aroque/) on December 21, 2023 2:23 pm
