# [Religion & Peace](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/)

## [A blog hosted by Hartford International University](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/)

[![Image 18: Hartford International University for Religion & Peace](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/wp-content/themes/hartford_seminary/library/images/hartford-logo.png)](https://www.hartfordinternational.edu/)

October 5th, 2022| Rev. Dr. David D. Grafton

## The Dilemma of the Role of Clergy and Interfaith Families

![Image 19: role of clergy in supporting interfaith families](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/27/2022/09/role-of-clergy-in-supporting-interfaith-families.jpg)

If it is true that America is becoming more publicly religiously plural, as sociological studies say, so then are American families. According to the [Pew Research Religious Landscape Survey of 2014](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2015/05/12/americas-changing-religious-landscape/), nearly four in ten Americans married since 2010 were married to a partner from a different religious tradition, compared to nineteen percent of religiously mixed marriages among those who married before 1960.

**The Rise of Interfaith Marriages**

The rise in religiously mixed marriages can certainly be attributed to the changing patterns of religious practice and identity among Americans. Because marrying for love is seen as an important ideal among Americans, we are willing to cross ethnic, cultural, and religious boundaries for the pursuit of love. It is just as common to see individuals “switch” to their partner’s religious tradition as remaining in their own tradition. This means that couples who remain active in their own religious tradition need to find ways to recognize, celebrate, and commemorate multiple religious holidays in their home. If one partner is Jewish and the other Christian, will they celebrate Passover _and_ Easter together? Will one attend services at church and the other at synagogue? What about when the extended family is involved? What will the family expectations be? If dietary restrictions are a part of the religious observance, will both refrain from certain foods or fast together?

Naomi Schaeffer Riley, in her book [_‘Til Faith Do Us Part: How Interfaith Marriage is Transforming America_](https://www.naomiriley.com/books/til-faith-do-us-part/)_,_ argues that there has been a dramatic cultural shift toward interfaith marriages, including among those communities that have traditionally forbidden or opposed such marriages. Riley makes the point that the vast majority of 18-to-23-year-olds do not believe it is important to marry someone from within your own religious tradition. Marrying for love is still the prominent ideal in American society. Riley points out what has become more publicly obvious, that there has been a generational shift across religious boundaries about views of marriage. Switching or mixing religious identities for love is part of the American cultural scene.

When you add children to the mix of these interfaith marriages there are more questions and more answers. Will the children be raised in one tradition or another, or both? Or, as is often the case, will they be raised in no tradition “until they can decide for themselves”? Riley notes that while interfaith couples may come to agreements about their personal religious practices when they are married, they continually renegotiate these decisions throughout the family’s journey. When the children are born, will they be baptized? Will they go to Hebrew school or Qur’an class? Will they attend Friday, Saturday, or Sunday services, or alternate? Will the family decorate the house for Christmas or Hanukkah, or both? Will the children observe religious dietary requirements if only one parent does? These questions continually come to the fore in each new phase of life.

**Religious Leaders Role in Supporting Interfaith Families**

If this is the reality of a current religiously plural America, how are clergy – or other religious leaders – responding? How are clergy reacting to these families in their communities when religious “switching, mixing and matching” is the norm? When an active member of the congregation’s son or daughter marries a Buddhist or Sikh, the congregation is now _de facto_ an interfaith community. Even if that interfaith couple decides to attend religious communities separately or none at all, the new relationship will continue to affect the extended family who remain within the congregation. It is no longer about “them” – it is now about “us.”

While leading a workshop among Christian clergy on interfaith relationships, the biggest topic my colleagues named was the ongoing frustration of not knowing how to support their interfaith families.

Knowing full well that couples are under duress from one partner or another, one extended family or another, or one’s larger religious tradition or another, how will clergy provide support for the spiritual well-being of the mixed-faith family? Because of their role, clergy will not only be sought after for advice by families, but they will also be triangulated to use their clerical authority: “Pastor, please tell my husband how important it is that Johnny be baptized.” Families will expect and hope for answers to their spiritually mixed realities.

Some Christian colleagues have also noted how interfaith couples have come to them and shared their apprehensions about how they will be received or treated by their religious community. Will they be included in congregational activities? Will it be okay if their children miss Sunday school because they are attending an Islamic Sunday school every other week? What happens if the children share about the family Hindu holiday celebrations in Sunday School? Some clergy have even reported being approached by other members of the congregation who want to know if the pastor agrees with the other religious tradition over their own faith. Does accepting the family into the congregation imply sanction of the other religious tradition? Clergy often are not sure how to respond when real families are involved.

Even those clergy who represent religious communities that do not support religiously mixed marriages are faced with pastoral decisions to either lay down the law, and then in all likelihood see the family leave their flock or break apart due to the stress, or to support the interfaith family and then to be included in the family process of navigating multiple religions. Some religious communities do not support religiously mixed marriages for a variety of reasons. Catholics, Mormons, Jews, and to some extent Muslims, have historically not “allowed” their members to marry outside their tradition. For some this is for spiritual reasons, for others it is simply a matter of keeping their religious tradition alive and viable. This prohibition or frowning on religiously mixed marriages, however, does not mean that these clergy are not in favor of positive interfaith relationships! In fact, quite often it is by fully embracing the traditions of these communities that clergy wish to participate in the public American religious pluralism.

**Lack of Clergy Training Leads to Lack of Support for Interfaith Families**

The unfortunate reality is that most clergy either publicly ignore the issue or try to attend to the spiritual needs of the family privately in ad hoc situations. Rarely is the issue addressed or named publicly. The most common reason for the silence among clergy is lack of preparation in ministerial training that leads to embarrassment and fear. Clergy are often embarrassed that they do not have the answers to these ongoing perplexing and complicated questions that interfaith families raise. And they are also afraid of what some of their members, other colleagues, or the larger religious denomination, will say to their allowing mixed religious marriages in their midst.

Clergy do not need to become interfaith experts, but they do need to become publicly comfortable with the multifaith reality of American society and their congregations. They do not need to have all the answers to family dilemmas, but they do need to become conversant in the language of interfaith marriages and families. To not address the issue is to abandon their own interfaith families and communities at exactly the moments when they need to feel spiritual guidance and support.

# [Religion & Peace](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/)

## [A blog hosted by Hartford International University](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/)

[![Image 18: Hartford International University for Religion & Peace](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/wp-content/themes/hartford_seminary/library/images/hartford-logo.png)](https://www.hartfordinternational.edu/)

October 5th, 2022| Rev. Dr. David D. Grafton

## The Dilemma of the Role of Clergy and Interfaith Families

![Image 19: role of clergy in supporting interfaith families](https://blog.hartfordinternational.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/27/2022/09/role-of-clergy-in-supporting-interfaith-families.jpg)

If it is true that America is becoming more publicly religiously plural, as sociological studies say, so then are American families. According to the [Pew Research Religious Landscape Survey of 2014](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2015/05/12/americas-changing-religious-landscape/), nearly four in ten Americans married since 2010 were married to a partner from a different religious tradition, compared to nineteen percent of religiously mixed marriages among those who married before 1960.

**The Rise of Interfaith Marriages**

The rise in religiously mixed marriages can certainly be attributed to the changing patterns of religious practice and identity among Americans. Because marrying for love is seen as an important ideal among Americans, we are willing to cross ethnic, cultural, and religious boundaries for the pursuit of love. It is just as common to see individuals “switch” to their partner’s religious tradition as remaining in their own tradition. This means that couples who remain active in their own religious tradition need to find ways to recognize, celebrate, and commemorate multiple religious holidays in their home. If one partner is Jewish and the other Christian, will they celebrate Passover _and_ Easter together? Will one attend services at church and the other at synagogue? What about when the extended family is involved? What will the family expectations be? If dietary restrictions are a part of the religious observance, will both refrain from certain foods or fast together?

Naomi Schaeffer Riley, in her book [_‘Til Faith Do Us Part: How Interfaith Marriage is Transforming America_](https://www.naomiriley.com/books/til-faith-do-us-part/)_,_ argues that there has been a dramatic cultural shift toward interfaith marriages, including among those communities that have traditionally forbidden or opposed such marriages. Riley makes the point that the vast majority of 18-to-23-year-olds do not believe it is important to marry someone from within your own religious tradition. Marrying for love is still the prominent ideal in American society. Riley points out what has become more publicly obvious, that there has been a generational shift across religious boundaries about views of marriage. Switching or mixing religious identities for love is part of the American cultural scene.

When you add children to the mix of these interfaith marriages there are more questions and more answers. Will the children be raised in one tradition or another, or both? Or, as is often the case, will they be raised in no tradition “until they can decide for themselves”? Riley notes that while interfaith couples may come to agreements about their personal religious practices when they are married, they continually renegotiate these decisions throughout the family’s journey. When the children are born, will they be baptized? Will they go to Hebrew school or Qur’an class? Will they attend Friday, Saturday, or Sunday services, or alternate? Will the family decorate the house for Christmas or Hanukkah, or both? Will the children observe religious dietary requirements if only one parent does? These questions continually come to the fore in each new phase of life.

**Religious Leaders Role in Supporting Interfaith Families**

If this is the reality of a current religiously plural America, how are clergy – or other religious leaders – responding? How are clergy reacting to these families in their communities when religious “switching, mixing and matching” is the norm? When an active member of the congregation’s son or daughter marries a Buddhist or Sikh, the congregation is now _de facto_ an interfaith community. Even if that interfaith couple decides to attend religious communities separately or none at all, the new relationship will continue to affect the extended family who remain within the congregation. It is no longer about “them” – it is now about “us.”

While leading a workshop among Christian clergy on interfaith relationships, the biggest topic my colleagues named was the ongoing frustration of not knowing how to support their interfaith families.

Knowing full well that couples are under duress from one partner or another, one extended family or another, or one’s larger religious tradition or another, how will clergy provide support for the spiritual well-being of the mixed-faith family? Because of their role, clergy will not only be sought after for advice by families, but they will also be triangulated to use their clerical authority: “Pastor, please tell my husband how important it is that Johnny be baptized.” Families will expect and hope for answers to their spiritually mixed realities.

Some Christian colleagues have also noted how interfaith couples have come to them and shared their apprehensions about how they will be received or treated by their religious community. Will they be included in congregational activities? Will it be okay if their children miss Sunday school because they are attending an Islamic Sunday school every other week? What happens if the children share about the family Hindu holiday celebrations in Sunday School? Some clergy have even reported being approached by other members of the congregation who want to know if the pastor agrees with the other religious tradition over their own faith. Does accepting the family into the congregation imply sanction of the other religious tradition? Clergy often are not sure how to respond when real families are involved.

Even those clergy who represent religious communities that do not support religiously mixed marriages are faced with pastoral decisions to either lay down the law, and then in all likelihood see the family leave their flock or break apart due to the stress, or to support the interfaith family and then to be included in the family process of navigating multiple religions. Some religious communities do not support religiously mixed marriages for a variety of reasons. Catholics, Mormons, Jews, and to some extent Muslims, have historically not “allowed” their members to marry outside their tradition. For some this is for spiritual reasons, for others it is simply a matter of keeping their religious tradition alive and viable. This prohibition or frowning on religiously mixed marriages, however, does not mean that these clergy are not in favor of positive interfaith relationships! In fact, quite often it is by fully embracing the traditions of these communities that clergy wish to participate in the public American religious pluralism.

**Lack of Clergy Training Leads to Lack of Support for Interfaith Families**

The unfortunate reality is that most clergy either publicly ignore the issue or try to attend to the spiritual needs of the family privately in ad hoc situations. Rarely is the issue addressed or named publicly. The most common reason for the silence among clergy is lack of preparation in ministerial training that leads to embarrassment and fear. Clergy are often embarrassed that they do not have the answers to these ongoing perplexing and complicated questions that interfaith families raise. And they are also afraid of what some of their members, other colleagues, or the larger religious denomination, will say to their allowing mixed religious marriages in their midst.

Clergy do not need to become interfaith experts, but they do need to become publicly comfortable with the multifaith reality of American society and their congregations. They do not need to have all the answers to family dilemmas, but they do need to become conversant in the language of interfaith marriages and families. To not address the issue is to abandon their own interfaith families and communities at exactly the moments when they need to feel spiritual guidance and support.

## ABSTRACT

This article offers the first empirical account of how a Religion and Worldviews approach to Religious Education (RE) prepares students to navigate worldview difference beyond school. Drawing on the experiences of 826 first-year undergraduates schooled in England and Wales, we explore how their experiences of ‘worldviews’ in the secondary school RE classroom relate to their readiness to engage with religion and worldview difference once they start university. Regression analysis reveals that worldview-related learning outcomes, specifically learning about the complex nature and internal diversity of religious and non-religious worldviews, as well as the role of personal decision-making in worldview formation, have the strongest positive relationships with a positive ‘pluralism orientation’ upon enrolment to undergraduate study. Perceived worldview diversity within the RE classroom is also important, highlighting the benefits of learning in contexts of assumed difference. Exploring differences by school type, level of RE studied, and students’ religious background, implications are drawn for national curriculum debates and pedagogical practice.

## Introduction

Recent debates around Religious Education (RE) curriculum reform have highlighted a disparity between young people’s lives and the current structures and practices supporting RE content and provision. The 2025 UK Department for Education’s _Curriculum and Assessment Review Final Report_ recognises that pupils ‘encounter a broader range of world views, including, for example, Humanism’ than they have done historically, yet states that RE has not kept pace with these social and cultural changes (Gov.uk Citation 2025, 108). Supportive of a form of RE that promotes pupil’s ‘intellectual, moral, social, and cultural development’ (46) the Review argues that, in many cases, RE as currently structured ‘does not prepare pupils adequately for life beyond school’ (108). Simultaneously, there is an ongoing movement towards a ‘Religion and Worldviews’ approach to RE, first proposed by the Commission on Religious Education (CoRE) in its 2018 report. Subsequent years have seen fierce debate about the proposal’s merits and how it might be most effectively put into practice, with debate focusing primarily on two areas. First, researchers have examined responses to the proposal and its practical implications for curriculum design, teacher expertise and classroom practice (British Humanist Association Citation 2015; Cooling, Bowie, and Panjwani Citation 2020; Everington Citation 2018; The Week Citation 2018). Second, scholars have explored the contested nature of ‘worldviews’ as a foundational concept, including debates over its definition, scope and application within RE (Hand Citation 2018; Humanists UK Citation 2018). However, little has been done to identify the long-term effects of a worldviews approach to RE, including its capacity to prepare students for the religious realities of post-school contexts.

In this article, we respond to the claims and recommendations made by both reports, examining new empirical data to explore how worldview engagement in the RE classroom equips students to positively navigate religious difference at university. Drawing on a survey of 826 UK university students who lived and went to secondary school in England and Wales prior to attending university, conducted at the time of first-year undergraduate enrolment (October–December 2022), we pursue two questions: 1. What aspects of a Religion and Worldviews approach do first-year UK university undergraduates recall experiencing in the school RE classroom? and 2. How, if at all, does a Religion and Worldviews approach prepare students for the challenges of relating to others different from themselves once they are at university?

## Literature review

### A Religion and Worldviews approach: the debate

The Commission on Religious Education (CoRE) published its 2018 report _Religion and Worldviews: The Way Forward_ following consultation with stakeholders including academics, RE teachers, education policy experts, secondary school pupils, and representatives from a range of religious communities. CoRE was established in 2016 by, but independent of, the Religious Education Council of England and Wales, to ‘review the legal, educational and policy frameworks for Religious Education (RE)’ (Commission on Religious Education Citation 2018, 19) and issue recommendations for its development. The Commission marshalled a mass of data to address challenges long acknowledged in schools, including a perception of the subject’s declining status, a lack of trained specialist teachers, and uneven quality of provision across the sector. Its primary concern was addressing how RE might better reflect twenty-first-century cultural realities, engaging more effectively with the lives of the young people who study it. The report recommends that RE be renamed ‘Religion and Worldviews’, and that students study a spectrum of religious and non-religious worldviews as a means of reflecting these cultural changes. This approach subsequently became highly influential in RE discourse, culminating in the RE Council of England and Wales publishing the ‘Religion and Worldviews Approach to RE Toolkit’, including guidance and suggested frameworks for curriculum design (Religious Education Council Citation 2024).

Much positive reaction to the Religion and Worldviews recommendations concerns inclusivity, pointing to how the language of ‘worldviews’ better captures life in the contemporary UK, in which the religiously observant are small in numbers and the majority identify as ‘non-religious’, especially younger generations. Incorporating ‘non-religious’ worldviews into RE reflects the recommendation by the _2004 National Framework for Religious Education_, a Qualifications and Curriculum Authority document drafted for the then Department for Education and Skills, that secular views be incorporated into English schools’ local syllabuses (Watson Citation 2008, Citation 2010) and echoes the British Humanist Association’s (Citation 2015) proposal for including non-religious worldviews in the curriculum (British Humanist Association Citation 2015). For its supporters, the approach has the benefit of reviving a sense of contemporary relevance and inclusivity for RE, which has suffered from traditional curricula that risk having limited meaning for young people today.

However, scepticism has emerged from other quarters, including some representatives of faith communities, such as The Board of Deputies of British Jews, who expressed during the initial debate surrounding the proposal that the inclusion of a range of worldviews is a dilution of the subject’s rigour (The Week Citation 2018). Cooling, Bowie, and Panjwani (Citation 2020, 36) summarise the tension: ‘Both the faith community objectors and Humanist supporters regard this as a victory for Humanism in the battle for space on the RE curriculum’. Other objections focus on practical issues. Everington’s (Citation 2018) qualitative research with twenty-five RE teachers in England highlights time constraints, a lack of resources, a lack of knowledge about the ‘non-religious’ among both specialist and non-specialist teachers, and the challenges of managing religious students who struggle to comprehend non-religious worldviews. Such concerns reflect worries about the adequacy of training for RE teachers to handle worldview diversity in the classroom.

Beyond these content-related and practical challenges, there are conceptual questions concerning the meaning, or classification, of ‘worldview’. ‘worldview’ is defined by CoRE in the Religion and Worldviews report as ‘a person’s way of understanding, experiencing and responding to the world’ (Commission on Religious Education Citation 2018, 26), derived ultimately from the German term _Weltanschauung_. Following critiques of the report’s terminology of ‘institutional worldviews’ as applied to the non-religious (see e.g. Hand Citation 2018; Humanists UK Citation 2018), subsequent work has been undertaken to clarify what we might understand ‘worldview’ to mean in the context of RE. Cooling, Bowie, and Panjwani (Citation 2020) suggest the proposed changes relate to a new _disciplinary framework_ of learning, rather than just content. They emphasise how this framework encompasses a recognition of the fluidity of worldviews, how worldviews are formed in interaction with one another, and how they are internally diverse rather than uniform. This approach allows religious and non-religious worldviews to be addressed in a way that reflects how they are _lived_, rather than rehearsing officially sanctioned or stereotypical portrayals that impede genuine understanding. More recent scholarship suggests that questions concerning the relationship between personal and institutional worldviews remain unresolved, with Plater (Citation 2025) proposing an alternative framework in which only individuals possess worldviews, while religions are understood as ‘communities of alignment’ (353) made up of ‘people who share ideas and practices in common’ (363). While these contributions differ in emphasis, they share a concern with distinguishing between interpretive worldview frameworks, and with the pedagogical implications of those distinctions.

Seven years since CoRE’s report stated that ‘the time is right for a new vision for the subject if we are to prepare children and young people for living in the increasingly diverse world in which they find themselves’ (2018: 6), the RE debate continues. The 2025 UK Department for Education’s _Curriculum and Assessment Review Final Report_ has drawn on stakeholders’ evidence to propose a staged approach to making RE a national curriculum subject, conceding that the Religious Education Council of England and Wales’ (Citation 2023) proposed National Content Standard for RE in England, which itself calls on the government to reform the subject based on CoRE’s work, ‘has potential as a catalyst for more substantial reform’ (Gov.uk Citation 2025, 109). Nevertheless, research continues to focus on perceived problems or benefits concerning the _content_ of RE, rather than its longer-term implications for individual development. Indeed, questions remain unanswered, including what role might RE play in helping young people engage in post-school contexts characterised by religious and cultural diversity? This is the concern of the present article.

### Life beyond the classroom: the UK university as a site of interfaith encounter

Encounters with religion and worldview difference are a daily reality for most university students in the UK. Just shy of 3 million people study at UK universities,Footnote 1 and for many, their university campus is a much more diverse space than their home community. Some meet students of other religions and worldviews for the first time. Others discover new channels for their beliefs, extending opportunities for expression, campaigning with, and meeting others of the same perspective (Aune, Perfect, and Ryan Citation 2024). Interactions with non-UK students are commonplace; international students make up a quarter of those studying at UK universities, and yearly international student enrolments have increased by almost 200,000 in the past five years.Footnote 2 As the frequency of encounters with the cultural ‘other’ increases, so too does the need for students to be able to relate positively across differences.

While university is a positive experience for most students, a minority experience hostility, insensitivity, coercion or discrimination (Weller, Hooley, and Moore Citation 2011; Peacock et al. Citation 2023). Such hostility, or fear of it, leads some students to conceal visible indicators of their religious identities. A National Union of Students’ survey of 9,229 higher and further education students found that one in five altered their appearance or behaviour for this reason, with instances highest among those of minority religions: Buddhists, Hindus, Jews and Muslims (National Union of Students NUS Citation 2012). This finding was echoed by Akel’s (Citation 2021) interviews with Muslim students at British universities and by Scott-Baumann et al.’s nation-wide study _Islam on Campus_ (Scott-Baumann et al. Citation 2020, 159), both revealing how Muslim students share a tendency to self-censor to avoid prejudice. Meanwhile, campus conflicts related to freedom of speech and religious expression remain commonplace, triggered or exacerbated by global events and national political tensions. There is little academic research on how students navigate these issues, despite significant increases in student protest and heightened Islamophobia and antisemitism since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 (Community Security Trust Citation 2024; Freeman Citation 2025; Tell MAMA Citation 2024).

Against this backdrop, higher education researchers have sought to understand how interfaith encounters happen within universities, so that they can be fostered in a way that cultivates mutual learning and respect, rather than hostility or division (Aune et al. Citation 2025; Fryer et al. Citation 2026; Peacock and Riggers-Piehl Citation 2025; Rockenbach et al. Citation 2015; Selznick et al. Citation 2022). Indeed, recent research has uncovered ways in which universities can maximise opportunities for relationship-building across religion and worldview lines (Aune et al. Citation 2025). However, little has been done to examine the pre-university experiences that best _prepare_ students for the realities of religious diversity on campus. Given the lively debate around the future of RE in England and Wales, our data on students’ experiences within the RE classroom present a timely opportunity to do just this.

## Conceptual framework: pluralism as ‘interfaith readiness’

If a goal of RE is to equip students with the skills and competencies required to relate well across difference in a diverse society, we must be clear on the framework through which we are measuring students’ ability to do this. This article adopts the framework of ‘pluralism’, one aspect of the ‘Interfaith Learning and Development’ model developed by Mayhew and Rockenbach (Citation 2021).

Mayhew and Rockenbach (Citation 2021) conceptualise Interfaith Learning and Development as a three-way measure of appreciative attitudes (towards specific religion or worldview groups), Self-Authored Worldview Commitment (SAWC) (‘students’ ability to make meaning of their own worldview identity in light of others’ worldviews’ Selznick et al. [Citation 2022: 308]), and pluralism. This article explores the latter, pluralism, which we define as students’ positive engagement with religion and worldview difference’ (Aune et al. Citation 2025).

Our theoretical basis for pluralism lies in the work of Eck (Citation 1993). Taking pluralism beyond the notion of the existence of different groups, and broadening it into an orientation involving behaviour and attitude, Eck proposes four aspects: ‘engagement with diversity rather than the sheer fact of diversity alone; migration from tolerance to acceptance of others; commitment as developmentally distinctive and possible within a relativistic society; and an understanding and appreciation of worldview differences (not merely commonalities)’ (Rockenbach et al. Citation 2015, 28). Following Mayhew and Rockenbach (Citation 2021), we operationalise pluralism via survey questions related to four sub-dimensions: global citizenship (seeking to understand and improve the lives of people across the world), goodwill towards others of different worldviews, appreciation of worldview commonalities and differences, and commitment to interfaith leadership and service.

US higher education research has explored pluralism within universities. Rockenbach et al. (Citation 2015) found that pluralism orientation scores are higher among students with minority religion and worldview perspectives (Buddhists, humanists, Jews, Muslims and those identifying as spiritual or agnostic), than among atheists and most Christians. In the first longitudinal higher education research on pluralism, Rockenbach and Mayhew (Citation 2024) found that students who gain in pluralism scores during higher education are those who are socially marginalised, for example due to sexuality or gender, and those without interfaith experience before university. They also found campus climate has an impact: growth in pluralism happens when campuses are welcoming to people of different religious and non-religious perspectives, support religion and spiritual expression (for example via prayer facilities or religious student groups) and provide opportunities to question and challenge their and others’ beliefs. Rockenbach and Mayhew’s work has been adapted to and replicated in the UK, with Aune et al. (Citation 2025) finding that three aspects of campus climate are associated with increases in pluralism: the perception that the university is religiously diverse, having safe spaces for spiritual expression, and provocative encounters, which challenge students’ assumptions about their own, and others’, worldviews. In this article, we are the first to measure students’ pluralism upon enrolment at university, before it is shaped by university life. We call this students’ ‘interfaith readiness’.

## Methods

### Data source and sample

The survey dataset used in this article represents the attitudes and behaviour related to religion and worldview diversity of 4,618 students studying at UK universities, collected between October and December 2022. The data were weighted using the Generalised Raking Method (Deville, Särndal, and Sautory Citation 1993) to ensure our sample reflected national student demographics. 2021–2022 data from the Higher Education Statistics Agency were used to align the sample with the national distributions for age, ethnicity, gender, institution type, level of study, and religious or worldview background. The sample used for this specific analysis consists of 826 first-year undergraduate students. These students’ ‘home region’, described in the survey as ‘where your family home is based or the area in which you were living before you started university’, include only England or Wales, to achieve a sample that best reflects those most likely to have their RE teaching influenced by curriculum debates discussed earlier.Footnote 3

Within our sample, most students (69.2%) attended a secondary school without a religious character.Footnote 4 Regarding the highest level of RE studied, GCSE was represented by the largest group (39%). Almost a quarter of our sample (24.4%) studied RE to A Level. Over half of our sample self-identified as non-religious (57.3%), and a further 22.9% Christian. Table 1 offers these characteristics in greater detail.

### Variables and analysis

To measure students’ reported engagement with a Religion and Worldviews approach to RE, we developed a set of seven Likert scale statements. We formulated the statement wording to reflect some of the considerations proposed in the 2018 CoRE report for the Religion and Worldviews curriculum, including the assertions that students ‘deserve to know that their own and their family’s worldview and community are acknowledged, even if they belong to a smaller community. If your own worldview is never mentioned, it is easy to conclude that you don’t count’, and that by the end of Key Stages 2 and 4, students should be learning about ‘the complex, diverse and plural nature of religious and non-religious worldviews’ (Commission on Religious Education Citation 2018, 74–75). Table 2 details our statements: one relates to assumptions of worldview difference in the classroom, two relate to experiences of sharing personal religious or non-religious worldviews and four are pedagogical, relating to learning outcomes.

### Table 2.  Items for students’ reported engagement with a Religion and worldviews approach during RE in school.*

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0002&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

We designed these items based on the assumption that students may not know their schools’ or teachers’ formal approach to RE; we asked them to reflect on their engagement with the concepts involved in the Religion and Worldviews approach, whether or not this approach was driven by external factors such as their school type, syllabus or teacher’s preferred style. In other words, regardless of whether the learning was intentional or grounded in formal curricular decisions made by a school, we are concerned with its consequences.

In the first analysis phase, we generated descriptive and bivariate statistics to ascertain the proportion of students who reported engaging in the seven Religion and Worldviews approach items. We conducted chi-square tests of associationFootnote 5 between the items and three student-related demographic variables: whether they attended a secondary school with a religious character, the highest level of RE studied, and their religion/worldview perspective. For the latter, due to the small sample size of religious minority students, we aggregated this variable into four categories: non-religious (57.3%), Christian (22.9%), minority religious students (including Hindu, Jewish, Muslim and Sikh students, 12.5%), and ‘other’ (7.3%).

In the second phase of analysis, we considered the Religion and Worldviews approach items as independent variables, exploring their association with students’ pluralism, or ‘interfaith readiness’ upon entering university, through a series of weighted multivariate Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analyses. In other words, we explored whether there was a statistically significant relationship between worldview-related experiences in the RE classroom and positive orientations towards pluralism at the point of entering university. To avoid multicollinearity in the regression analyses, we ran a reliability test on the four Likert scale statements related to learning outcomes. Noting high levels of correlation, we combined these items into one variable we treat as continuous, called ‘Worldviews learning outcomes’ (a = .841).Footnote 6

The dependent variables for the OLS regression analyses were students’ pluralism scores, a construct consisting of multiple items that represent the extent to which students actively engage in religion and worldview diversity (see Conceptual Framework section). The survey statements were divided into four variables: a) global citizenship, b) goodwill towards those of other religions and worldviews, c) appreciation of interreligious commonalities and differences, and d) commitment to interfaith leadership and service (see Table 3).

### Table 3.  Items for OLS regression-dependent variables, ‘pluralism orientation’ subscales.*

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0003&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

In line with previous literature that employs this measure (Rockenbach et al. Citation 2020; Aune et al. Citation 2025), we combined the sub-scales with four additional statements to create an additional variable, ‘overall pluralism orientation’. The four additional statements concerned relationships across difference: ‘It is possible to have strong relationships with those of religiously diverse backgrounds and still strongly believe in my own worldview’, ‘My faith or beliefs are strengthened by relationships with those of diverse religious and non-religious backgrounds’, ‘I am open to adjusting my beliefs as I learn from other people and have new life experiences’, and ‘I try to build relationships with people who hold religious or non-religious beliefs that I disagree with’. The five final dependent measures, as well as our independent measure of ‘Worldviews learning outcomes’ were standardised (with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1) for the analysis. We ran five regression models, considering the role of students’ self-reported experiences of worldviews in the RE classroom in relation to each pluralism variable in turn.

## Results and discussion

### Reported engagement in a Religion and Worldviews approach

We first asked what aspects of a Religion and Worldviews approach do first-year UK university undergraduates recall experiencing in the school RE classroom? Table 4 presents the frequency and proportion of students who report experiencing different aspects of worldviews-style engagement.

### Table 4.  Frequency of first year UK university undergraduate students who agreed that they engaged in different worldviews-style teaching and learning in the school RE classroom (_N_ = 826).

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0004&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

Several key observations emerge from these figures. Notably, higher proportions of students reported experiences of ‘worldviews’ style RE in relation to the final four statements – those concerned with learning outcomes – than the first three statements reporting student diversity and the affirming of one’s own worldview within the RE classroom. Indeed, while ‘worldviews’ appeared prominently in relation to teaching and learning, this only translated into discussion of their own worldview – whether religious or non-religious – for half (50.5%) of students. This could be attributed to learning styles and different levels of confidence among pupils, but suggests something other than full inclusion of pupils’ own worldview identities within the RE classroom. This unevenness is reinforced by the fact that only 56.7% felt their worldview was respected in this context. While the high proportion of ‘neither agree nor disagree’ responses (29.7%) warns against inferring patterns of widespread hostility, this does suggest open affirmation and recognition of worldviews represented in the RE classroom is variable and selective. Nevertheless, the fact ‘agree’ responses make up a majority of responses for each statement suggests the worldviews style of RE has become – or at least is becoming – normative across schools in England and Wales. This may indicate a deliberate adoption of a worldviews approach to RE curricula by a teacher, or the presence of associated assumptions in the class experience as a consequence of ‘worldviews’ language resonating with wider cultural norms. The disparate and partial adoption of worldviews RE across the sector suggests a combination of the two is most likely.

Statistically significant results from the subsequent chi-square tests of association revealed notable patterns of engagement with a worldviews approach across several variables. First, students who attended secondary schools with a religious character were more likely to feel engaged in classroom discussions than those who attended schools without a religious character. But they were also more likely to feel excluded in other ways. They were more likely than their peers in non-religious schools to report that they had talked about their own worldview in class (60.3% vs. 48.1%) and that they had learnt about the complexity of both religious and non-religious perspectives (73.9% vs. 63.2%). Yet they were also more likely to report _disagreement_ that their worldviews were respected (21.8% vs. 10.7%) and that they had studied alongside classmates with diverse beliefs (27.3% vs. 22.6%). They were also more likely to disagree that worldviews can be shaped by personal decisions as well as tradition (12.1% vs. 9.2%).

Second, the stage of study influenced experiences. Students who had studied RE at AS or A Level reported higher levels of agreement with the statements than those who only studied RE until GCSE or Year 9. They were more likely to say they studied alongside classmates with a range of worldviews (73% vs. 59.6% GCSE and 54.5% Year 9), to have talked about their own worldview in the RE classroom (57.9% vs. 51.4% and 44.6%), and to feel that their personal perspectives were respected (66.7% vs. 55% and 51.7%). These findings suggest that longer and more advanced engagement with RE is associated with richer classroom experiences, rather than just greater factual knowledge.

Lastly, religious identity was statistically significant. Both Christian and minority religious students reported greater engagement in a worldviews approach than non-religious students. A clear majority of minority religious students (79.3%) and Christians (61.3%) reported that they studied alongside classmates with a range of religious and non-religious worldviews, compared with 56.1% of non-religious students. Similarly, 71.3% of minority religious students and 51.8% of Christian students reported talking about their own worldview in class, compared with 47% of non-religious students. Feelings of respect followed the same pattern: 74% of minority religious students and 57% of Christians felt their worldviews were respected, compared with 55.9% of non-religious students. This pattern suggests that the RE classroom can be a more affirming and validating place for religious students, perhaps because the subject matter as currently framed resonates more closely with their lived experiences, or the opportunities to share and have their perspectives respected offer a sense of visibility missing elsewhere in school. By contrast, lower levels of engagement among non-religious students highlight a potential imbalance in the way that RE is currently framed, one that risks reinforcing the voices of religious students to the exclusion of others.

### The relationship between worldview engagement and ‘interfaith readiness’

We then asked, how, and to what extent, does a Religion and Worldviews approach prepare students for the challenges of relating to others different from themselves at university? Table 5 provides the results of the OLS regression analyses exploring the relationship between students’ engagement in worldviews in the RE classroom and their baseline measure of pluralism (including the ‘overall pluralism orientation’ variable, alongside the four sub-scales) upon enrolling in their undergraduate studies at university.

### Table 5.  OLS regressions indicating the relationship between worldviews-related engagement in the RE classroom and students’ baseline measures of pluralism upon enrolment at university (_N_ = 824–825).

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0005&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

The most consistently and strongly significant predictor of pluralism was students’ worldviews learning outcomes, reinforcing the notion that _what_ students learn in RE remains key. Students who reported learning in RE that worldviews can be religious or non-religious, that both religious and non-religious worldviews are shaped not only by tradition but by personal decisions, that such worldviews are internally complex, and that there is diversity within religious and non-religious traditions demonstrated higher levels of all of our measures of pluralism upon enrolment to university. While we cannot directly infer causality, this pattern suggests that worldviews-related content, whether intentionally taught or not, may be particularly influential, lending empirical support to CoRE’s 2018 call for a substantive and formalised curricular shift towards RE teaching that foregrounds the diversity, complexity, and lived nature of both religious and non-religious worldviews. Moreover, in response to the 2025 Curriculum Review’s claim that ‘RE in many schools is not good enough and does not prepare pupils adequately for life beyond school’ (Gov.uk Citation 2025, 108), these findings help to specify _what kinds of learning_ within RE may best contribute to students’ readiness to engage in post-school environments characterised by diverse worldview communities. Namely, reforms grounded in a worldviews approach are likely to support precisely this.

Alongside learning outcomes, the perception of diversity within the RE classroom consistently predicted students’ pluralism upon entering university, with the exception of global citizenship. In other words, students who perceived their school RE classrooms as spaces where a range of religious and non-religious worldviews were represented were more likely to demonstrate readiness to engage across worldview differences at university. This finding resonates with previous research linking perceived diversity to pluralistic attitudes (Bowman Citation 2012; Aune et al. Citation 2025), suggesting that learning RE within a context of assumed difference, where diversity is expected, rather than exceptional, positively shapes students’ preparedness for diversity in non-classroom contexts.

A more puzzling finding concerns the negative relationship between feeling that one’s own worldview is respected in the RE classroom and outcomes related to global citizenship. Whilst this finding appears counterintuitive, and in opposition to previous work that links insensitivity to decreases in interfaith learning (Aune et al. Citation 2025; Rockenbach et al. Citation 2015) other work suggests that experiences of perceived insensitivity may prompt reflective learning and deeper engagement with difference (Peacock and Riggers-Piehl Citation 2025). Ultimately, we must interpret this finding with caution. It is inappropriate to conclude that diminished respect or insensitivity should be used as a pedagogical strategy in RE. Instead, the challenge is to identify alternative ways of creating constructive encounters that stretch students to engage with difference – a concept we call ‘provocative encounters’ in other analyses (Aune et al. Citation 2025; Fryer et al. Citation 2026) – while ensuring that respect and inclusion remain core principles of RE.

## Conclusion, limitations and implications

We sought to answer two questions: 1. What aspects of a Religion and Worldviews approach do first-year UK university undergraduates recall experiencing in the school RE classroom? and 2. How, if at all, does a Religion and Worldviews approach prepare students for the challenges of relating to others different from themselves once they are at university?

In response to our first question, we found that while the concept of worldviews appears increasingly embedded in what is taught in the RE classroom, reports of discussion of one’s own personal worldviews, and the perception among students that personal worldviews are respected, are less consistent. Engagement varies by school type, stage of study, and religious identity, suggesting that whilst a worldviews approach to RE may be becoming normative in terms of content, it remains uneven in practice.

Responding to our second question, our analysis revealed strong positive relationships between worldview-related learning outcomes (for example, learning about the complex nature and internal diversity of religious and non-religious worldviews), and students’ ‘interfaith readiness’ on entry to university. Perceived worldview diversity within the RE classroom is also significant, highlighting the benefits of learning in contexts of assumed difference.

We acknowledge several limitations when interpreting these findings. Across our five regression models, R 2 values ranged from .110 to .242, indicating that the RE experiences accounted for between 11% and 24.2% of the variance in students’ pluralism on entry to university. This means that, as we might reasonably expect, a substantial proportion of variance is explained by other factors, such as personal characteristics, school-level influences, and wider social contexts. Moreover, our sample size precluded a multilevel modelling approach, which would have generated a more nuanced examination of the interaction between individual- and school-level variables. Future research drawing on a larger sample would increase statistical power and allow for this modelling.

Our findings present other avenues for future research, including that which explores the consequences of talking about personal worldviews and feeling that one’s worldview is respected; these are the aspects of the RE classroom fewest students reported experiencing, and their relationship with students’ ‘interfaith readiness’ is unclear. Moreover, pluralism orientation is but one aspect of ‘interfaith readiness’. We might reasonably expect that the independent variables might interact differently with the other two outcomes used in the Interfaith Learning and Development conceptual framework: ‘self authored worldview commitment (reflexively constructing personal worldviews in dialogue with those that are different) and appreciative attitudes towards named religious groups different from one’s own (Mayhew and Rockenbach Citation 2021). Research that explores the role of RE in students’ interfaith learning development across all three domains would be beneficial.

We suggest that adapting RE to reflect a plurality of religious and non-religious worldview orientations is not just a matter of representation or inclusion, but one that has meaningful educational and social consequences for students when they leave school. As such, we draw implications from our findings for RE professionals. First, there is a need for RE teachers and curriculum or syllabus designers to ensure that non-religious perspectives are given appropriate weight alongside religious ones. This means not only teaching about secular and humanist perspectives, but encouraging non-religious students to articulate their views in a space that feels safe and respected.

Second, schools with a religious character should be more intentional about drawing on diverse perspectives, particularly non-religious ones, to ensure all students feel represented. Creating classroom spaces in which worldviews are explored beyond the dominant tradition could help balance opportunities for personal reflection with a stronger sense of belonging. These first two recommendations build on others’ work on non-religious students’ experiences of RE, such as Strhan and Shillitoe (Citation 2022), who argue that many non-religious pupils experience a ‘hermeneutic injustice’ (2022: 261) due to them ‘not being given meaningful opportunities to explore their own worldviews’ in the RE classroom (263).

Third, for schools situated in more religiously and culturally homogeneous areas, where it is difficult to assume diversity through classroom demographics alone, a range of religious and non-religious perspectives need to be intentionally integrated into curriculum content and pedagogy. We recognise this as a balancing act; whilst teachers must acknowledge and affirm the diversity that is present in the pupil body, they must also recognise where diversity is absent, avoiding framing diverse perspectives in ways that feel remote or abstract. Casson et al. (Citation 2023) study of the rural church primary school illustrates this. They emphasise the need for ‘attention to the context of each rural parish, and community’, recognising that rural school communities may draw pupils from dispersed catchment areas and that connections are often ‘brittle and fragile’ (2023: 105). Effective practice therefore needs careful pedagogical reflection on how difference is constructed and/or foregrounded in order to support students in engaging with perspectives that are not explicitly represented in their peer group.

Lastly, our key finding from the regression analyses, that worldview-related learning outcomes are associated with greater pluralism upon starting university, raises important implications for assessment. If outcomes framed in this analysis, such as understanding the internal complexity of religious and non-religious worldviews, or recognising the role of personal decision-making in worldview formation, are educationally consequential, then existing models of assessment may well be insufficient. Whilst specific recommendations for assessment fall outside the remit of this paper, we would endorse a framework that captures interpretive and reflexive forms of learning. Emerging models of religious literacy that foreground worldview complexity, positionality, and encounter with plurality, such as Shaw’s concept of ‘worldview literacy’ (Shaw Citation 2022), may offer a productive starting point for rethinking how learning in RE is conceptualised and measured.

## ABSTRACT

This article offers the first empirical account of how a Religion and Worldviews approach to Religious Education (RE) prepares students to navigate worldview difference beyond school. Drawing on the experiences of 826 first-year undergraduates schooled in England and Wales, we explore how their experiences of ‘worldviews’ in the secondary school RE classroom relate to their readiness to engage with religion and worldview difference once they start university. Regression analysis reveals that worldview-related learning outcomes, specifically learning about the complex nature and internal diversity of religious and non-religious worldviews, as well as the role of personal decision-making in worldview formation, have the strongest positive relationships with a positive ‘pluralism orientation’ upon enrolment to undergraduate study. Perceived worldview diversity within the RE classroom is also important, highlighting the benefits of learning in contexts of assumed difference. Exploring differences by school type, level of RE studied, and students’ religious background, implications are drawn for national curriculum debates and pedagogical practice.

## Introduction

Recent debates around Religious Education (RE) curriculum reform have highlighted a disparity between young people’s lives and the current structures and practices supporting RE content and provision. The 2025 UK Department for Education’s _Curriculum and Assessment Review Final Report_ recognises that pupils ‘encounter a broader range of world views, including, for example, Humanism’ than they have done historically, yet states that RE has not kept pace with these social and cultural changes (Gov.uk Citation 2025, 108). Supportive of a form of RE that promotes pupil’s ‘intellectual, moral, social, and cultural development’ (46) the Review argues that, in many cases, RE as currently structured ‘does not prepare pupils adequately for life beyond school’ (108). Simultaneously, there is an ongoing movement towards a ‘Religion and Worldviews’ approach to RE, first proposed by the Commission on Religious Education (CoRE) in its 2018 report. Subsequent years have seen fierce debate about the proposal’s merits and how it might be most effectively put into practice, with debate focusing primarily on two areas. First, researchers have examined responses to the proposal and its practical implications for curriculum design, teacher expertise and classroom practice (British Humanist Association Citation 2015; Cooling, Bowie, and Panjwani Citation 2020; Everington Citation 2018; The Week Citation 2018). Second, scholars have explored the contested nature of ‘worldviews’ as a foundational concept, including debates over its definition, scope and application within RE (Hand Citation 2018; Humanists UK Citation 2018). However, little has been done to identify the long-term effects of a worldviews approach to RE, including its capacity to prepare students for the religious realities of post-school contexts.

In this article, we respond to the claims and recommendations made by both reports, examining new empirical data to explore how worldview engagement in the RE classroom equips students to positively navigate religious difference at university. Drawing on a survey of 826 UK university students who lived and went to secondary school in England and Wales prior to attending university, conducted at the time of first-year undergraduate enrolment (October–December 2022), we pursue two questions: 1. What aspects of a Religion and Worldviews approach do first-year UK university undergraduates recall experiencing in the school RE classroom? and 2. How, if at all, does a Religion and Worldviews approach prepare students for the challenges of relating to others different from themselves once they are at university?

## Literature review

### A Religion and Worldviews approach: the debate

The Commission on Religious Education (CoRE) published its 2018 report _Religion and Worldviews: The Way Forward_ following consultation with stakeholders including academics, RE teachers, education policy experts, secondary school pupils, and representatives from a range of religious communities. CoRE was established in 2016 by, but independent of, the Religious Education Council of England and Wales, to ‘review the legal, educational and policy frameworks for Religious Education (RE)’ (Commission on Religious Education Citation 2018, 19) and issue recommendations for its development. The Commission marshalled a mass of data to address challenges long acknowledged in schools, including a perception of the subject’s declining status, a lack of trained specialist teachers, and uneven quality of provision across the sector. Its primary concern was addressing how RE might better reflect twenty-first-century cultural realities, engaging more effectively with the lives of the young people who study it. The report recommends that RE be renamed ‘Religion and Worldviews’, and that students study a spectrum of religious and non-religious worldviews as a means of reflecting these cultural changes. This approach subsequently became highly influential in RE discourse, culminating in the RE Council of England and Wales publishing the ‘Religion and Worldviews Approach to RE Toolkit’, including guidance and suggested frameworks for curriculum design (Religious Education Council Citation 2024).

Much positive reaction to the Religion and Worldviews recommendations concerns inclusivity, pointing to how the language of ‘worldviews’ better captures life in the contemporary UK, in which the religiously observant are small in numbers and the majority identify as ‘non-religious’, especially younger generations. Incorporating ‘non-religious’ worldviews into RE reflects the recommendation by the _2004 National Framework for Religious Education_, a Qualifications and Curriculum Authority document drafted for the then Department for Education and Skills, that secular views be incorporated into English schools’ local syllabuses (Watson Citation 2008, Citation 2010) and echoes the British Humanist Association’s (Citation 2015) proposal for including non-religious worldviews in the curriculum (British Humanist Association Citation 2015). For its supporters, the approach has the benefit of reviving a sense of contemporary relevance and inclusivity for RE, which has suffered from traditional curricula that risk having limited meaning for young people today.

However, scepticism has emerged from other quarters, including some representatives of faith communities, such as The Board of Deputies of British Jews, who expressed during the initial debate surrounding the proposal that the inclusion of a range of worldviews is a dilution of the subject’s rigour (The Week Citation 2018). Cooling, Bowie, and Panjwani (Citation 2020, 36) summarise the tension: ‘Both the faith community objectors and Humanist supporters regard this as a victory for Humanism in the battle for space on the RE curriculum’. Other objections focus on practical issues. Everington’s (Citation 2018) qualitative research with twenty-five RE teachers in England highlights time constraints, a lack of resources, a lack of knowledge about the ‘non-religious’ among both specialist and non-specialist teachers, and the challenges of managing religious students who struggle to comprehend non-religious worldviews. Such concerns reflect worries about the adequacy of training for RE teachers to handle worldview diversity in the classroom.

Beyond these content-related and practical challenges, there are conceptual questions concerning the meaning, or classification, of ‘worldview’. ‘worldview’ is defined by CoRE in the Religion and Worldviews report as ‘a person’s way of understanding, experiencing and responding to the world’ (Commission on Religious Education Citation 2018, 26), derived ultimately from the German term _Weltanschauung_. Following critiques of the report’s terminology of ‘institutional worldviews’ as applied to the non-religious (see e.g. Hand Citation 2018; Humanists UK Citation 2018), subsequent work has been undertaken to clarify what we might understand ‘worldview’ to mean in the context of RE. Cooling, Bowie, and Panjwani (Citation 2020) suggest the proposed changes relate to a new _disciplinary framework_ of learning, rather than just content. They emphasise how this framework encompasses a recognition of the fluidity of worldviews, how worldviews are formed in interaction with one another, and how they are internally diverse rather than uniform. This approach allows religious and non-religious worldviews to be addressed in a way that reflects how they are _lived_, rather than rehearsing officially sanctioned or stereotypical portrayals that impede genuine understanding. More recent scholarship suggests that questions concerning the relationship between personal and institutional worldviews remain unresolved, with Plater (Citation 2025) proposing an alternative framework in which only individuals possess worldviews, while religions are understood as ‘communities of alignment’ (353) made up of ‘people who share ideas and practices in common’ (363). While these contributions differ in emphasis, they share a concern with distinguishing between interpretive worldview frameworks, and with the pedagogical implications of those distinctions.

Seven years since CoRE’s report stated that ‘the time is right for a new vision for the subject if we are to prepare children and young people for living in the increasingly diverse world in which they find themselves’ (2018: 6), the RE debate continues. The 2025 UK Department for Education’s _Curriculum and Assessment Review Final Report_ has drawn on stakeholders’ evidence to propose a staged approach to making RE a national curriculum subject, conceding that the Religious Education Council of England and Wales’ (Citation 2023) proposed National Content Standard for RE in England, which itself calls on the government to reform the subject based on CoRE’s work, ‘has potential as a catalyst for more substantial reform’ (Gov.uk Citation 2025, 109). Nevertheless, research continues to focus on perceived problems or benefits concerning the _content_ of RE, rather than its longer-term implications for individual development. Indeed, questions remain unanswered, including what role might RE play in helping young people engage in post-school contexts characterised by religious and cultural diversity? This is the concern of the present article.

### Life beyond the classroom: the UK university as a site of interfaith encounter

Encounters with religion and worldview difference are a daily reality for most university students in the UK. Just shy of 3 million people study at UK universities,Footnote 1 and for many, their university campus is a much more diverse space than their home community. Some meet students of other religions and worldviews for the first time. Others discover new channels for their beliefs, extending opportunities for expression, campaigning with, and meeting others of the same perspective (Aune, Perfect, and Ryan Citation 2024). Interactions with non-UK students are commonplace; international students make up a quarter of those studying at UK universities, and yearly international student enrolments have increased by almost 200,000 in the past five years.Footnote 2 As the frequency of encounters with the cultural ‘other’ increases, so too does the need for students to be able to relate positively across differences.

While university is a positive experience for most students, a minority experience hostility, insensitivity, coercion or discrimination (Weller, Hooley, and Moore Citation 2011; Peacock et al. Citation 2023). Such hostility, or fear of it, leads some students to conceal visible indicators of their religious identities. A National Union of Students’ survey of 9,229 higher and further education students found that one in five altered their appearance or behaviour for this reason, with instances highest among those of minority religions: Buddhists, Hindus, Jews and Muslims (National Union of Students NUS Citation 2012). This finding was echoed by Akel’s (Citation 2021) interviews with Muslim students at British universities and by Scott-Baumann et al.’s nation-wide study _Islam on Campus_ (Scott-Baumann et al. Citation 2020, 159), both revealing how Muslim students share a tendency to self-censor to avoid prejudice. Meanwhile, campus conflicts related to freedom of speech and religious expression remain commonplace, triggered or exacerbated by global events and national political tensions. There is little academic research on how students navigate these issues, despite significant increases in student protest and heightened Islamophobia and antisemitism since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 (Community Security Trust Citation 2024; Freeman Citation 2025; Tell MAMA Citation 2024).

Against this backdrop, higher education researchers have sought to understand how interfaith encounters happen within universities, so that they can be fostered in a way that cultivates mutual learning and respect, rather than hostility or division (Aune et al. Citation 2025; Fryer et al. Citation 2026; Peacock and Riggers-Piehl Citation 2025; Rockenbach et al. Citation 2015; Selznick et al. Citation 2022). Indeed, recent research has uncovered ways in which universities can maximise opportunities for relationship-building across religion and worldview lines (Aune et al. Citation 2025). However, little has been done to examine the pre-university experiences that best _prepare_ students for the realities of religious diversity on campus. Given the lively debate around the future of RE in England and Wales, our data on students’ experiences within the RE classroom present a timely opportunity to do just this.

## Conceptual framework: pluralism as ‘interfaith readiness’

If a goal of RE is to equip students with the skills and competencies required to relate well across difference in a diverse society, we must be clear on the framework through which we are measuring students’ ability to do this. This article adopts the framework of ‘pluralism’, one aspect of the ‘Interfaith Learning and Development’ model developed by Mayhew and Rockenbach (Citation 2021).

Mayhew and Rockenbach (Citation 2021) conceptualise Interfaith Learning and Development as a three-way measure of appreciative attitudes (towards specific religion or worldview groups), Self-Authored Worldview Commitment (SAWC) (‘students’ ability to make meaning of their own worldview identity in light of others’ worldviews’ Selznick et al. [Citation 2022: 308]), and pluralism. This article explores the latter, pluralism, which we define as students’ positive engagement with religion and worldview difference’ (Aune et al. Citation 2025).

Our theoretical basis for pluralism lies in the work of Eck (Citation 1993). Taking pluralism beyond the notion of the existence of different groups, and broadening it into an orientation involving behaviour and attitude, Eck proposes four aspects: ‘engagement with diversity rather than the sheer fact of diversity alone; migration from tolerance to acceptance of others; commitment as developmentally distinctive and possible within a relativistic society; and an understanding and appreciation of worldview differences (not merely commonalities)’ (Rockenbach et al. Citation 2015, 28). Following Mayhew and Rockenbach (Citation 2021), we operationalise pluralism via survey questions related to four sub-dimensions: global citizenship (seeking to understand and improve the lives of people across the world), goodwill towards others of different worldviews, appreciation of worldview commonalities and differences, and commitment to interfaith leadership and service.

US higher education research has explored pluralism within universities. Rockenbach et al. (Citation 2015) found that pluralism orientation scores are higher among students with minority religion and worldview perspectives (Buddhists, humanists, Jews, Muslims and those identifying as spiritual or agnostic), than among atheists and most Christians. In the first longitudinal higher education research on pluralism, Rockenbach and Mayhew (Citation 2024) found that students who gain in pluralism scores during higher education are those who are socially marginalised, for example due to sexuality or gender, and those without interfaith experience before university. They also found campus climate has an impact: growth in pluralism happens when campuses are welcoming to people of different religious and non-religious perspectives, support religion and spiritual expression (for example via prayer facilities or religious student groups) and provide opportunities to question and challenge their and others’ beliefs. Rockenbach and Mayhew’s work has been adapted to and replicated in the UK, with Aune et al. (Citation 2025) finding that three aspects of campus climate are associated with increases in pluralism: the perception that the university is religiously diverse, having safe spaces for spiritual expression, and provocative encounters, which challenge students’ assumptions about their own, and others’, worldviews. In this article, we are the first to measure students’ pluralism upon enrolment at university, before it is shaped by university life. We call this students’ ‘interfaith readiness’.

## Methods

### Data source and sample

The survey dataset used in this article represents the attitudes and behaviour related to religion and worldview diversity of 4,618 students studying at UK universities, collected between October and December 2022. The data were weighted using the Generalised Raking Method (Deville, Särndal, and Sautory Citation 1993) to ensure our sample reflected national student demographics. 2021–2022 data from the Higher Education Statistics Agency were used to align the sample with the national distributions for age, ethnicity, gender, institution type, level of study, and religious or worldview background. The sample used for this specific analysis consists of 826 first-year undergraduate students. These students’ ‘home region’, described in the survey as ‘where your family home is based or the area in which you were living before you started university’, include only England or Wales, to achieve a sample that best reflects those most likely to have their RE teaching influenced by curriculum debates discussed earlier.Footnote 3

Within our sample, most students (69.2%) attended a secondary school without a religious character.Footnote 4 Regarding the highest level of RE studied, GCSE was represented by the largest group (39%). Almost a quarter of our sample (24.4%) studied RE to A Level. Over half of our sample self-identified as non-religious (57.3%), and a further 22.9% Christian.
