### Variables and analysis

To measure students’ reported engagement with a Religion and Worldviews approach to RE, we developed a set of seven Likert scale statements. We formulated the statement wording to reflect some of the considerations proposed in the 2018 CoRE report for the Religion and Worldviews curriculum, including the assertions that students ‘deserve to know that their own and their family’s worldview and community are acknowledged, even if they belong to a smaller community. If your own worldview is never mentioned, it is easy to conclude that you don’t count’, and that by the end of Key Stages 2 and 4, students should be learning about ‘the complex, diverse and plural nature of religious and non-religious worldviews’ (Commission on Religious Education Citation 2018, 74–75). Table 2 details our statements: one relates to assumptions of worldview difference in the classroom, two relate to experiences of sharing personal religious or non-religious worldviews and four are pedagogical, relating to learning outcomes.

### Table 2.  Items for students’ reported engagement with a Religion and worldviews approach during RE in school.*

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0002&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

We designed these items based on the assumption that students may not know their schools’ or teachers’ formal approach to RE; we asked them to reflect on their engagement with the concepts involved in the Religion and Worldviews approach, whether or not this approach was driven by external factors such as their school type, syllabus or teacher’s preferred style. In other words, regardless of whether the learning was intentional or grounded in formal curricular decisions made by a school, we are concerned with its consequences.

In the first analysis phase, we generated descriptive and bivariate statistics to ascertain the proportion of students who reported engaging in the seven Religion and Worldviews approach items. We conducted chi-square tests of associationFootnote 5 between the items and three student-related demographic variables: whether they attended a secondary school with a religious character, the highest level of RE studied, and their religion/worldview perspective. For the latter, due to the small sample size of religious minority students, we aggregated this variable into four categories: non-religious (57.3%), Christian (22.9%), minority religious students (including Hindu, Jewish, Muslim and Sikh students, 12.5%), and ‘other’ (7.3%).

In the second phase of analysis, we considered the Religion and Worldviews approach items as independent variables, exploring their association with students’ pluralism, or ‘interfaith readiness’ upon entering university, through a series of weighted multivariate Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analyses. In other words, we explored whether there was a statistically significant relationship between worldview-related experiences in the RE classroom and positive orientations towards pluralism at the point of entering university. To avoid multicollinearity in the regression analyses, we ran a reliability test on the four Likert scale statements related to learning outcomes. Noting high levels of correlation, we combined these items into one variable we treat as continuous, called ‘Worldviews learning outcomes’ (a = .841).Footnote 6

The dependent variables for the OLS regression analyses were students’ pluralism scores, a construct consisting of multiple items that represent the extent to which students actively engage in religion and worldview diversity (see Conceptual Framework section). The survey statements were divided into four variables: a) global citizenship, b) goodwill towards those of other religions and worldviews, c) appreciation of interreligious commonalities and differences, and d) commitment to interfaith leadership and service (see Table 3).

### Table 3.  Items for OLS regression-dependent variables, ‘pluralism orientation’ subscales.*

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0003&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

In line with previous literature that employs this measure (Rockenbach et al. Citation 2020; Aune et al. Citation 2025), we combined the sub-scales with four additional statements to create an additional variable, ‘overall pluralism orientation’. The four additional statements concerned relationships across difference: ‘It is possible to have strong relationships with those of religiously diverse backgrounds and still strongly believe in my own worldview’, ‘My faith or beliefs are strengthened by relationships with those of diverse religious and non-religious backgrounds’, ‘I am open to adjusting my beliefs as I learn from other people and have new life experiences’, and ‘I try to build relationships with people who hold religious or non-religious beliefs that I disagree with’. The five final dependent measures, as well as our independent measure of ‘Worldviews learning outcomes’ were standardised (with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1) for the analysis. We ran five regression models, considering the role of students’ self-reported experiences of worldviews in the RE classroom in relation to each pluralism variable in turn.

## Results and discussion

### Reported engagement in a Religion and Worldviews approach

We first asked what aspects of a Religion and Worldviews approach do first-year UK university undergraduates recall experiencing in the school RE classroom? Table 4 presents the frequency and proportion of students who report experiencing different aspects of worldviews-style engagement.

### Table 4.  Frequency of first year UK university undergraduate students who agreed that they engaged in different worldviews-style teaching and learning in the school RE classroom (_N_ = 826).

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0004&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

Several key observations emerge from these figures. Notably, higher proportions of students reported experiences of ‘worldviews’ style RE in relation to the final four statements – those concerned with learning outcomes – than the first three statements reporting student diversity and the affirming of one’s own worldview within the RE classroom. Indeed, while ‘worldviews’ appeared prominently in relation to teaching and learning, this only translated into discussion of their own worldview – whether religious or non-religious – for half (50.5%) of students. This could be attributed to learning styles and different levels of confidence among pupils, but suggests something other than full inclusion of pupils’ own worldview identities within the RE classroom. This unevenness is reinforced by the fact that only 56.7% felt their worldview was respected in this context. While the high proportion of ‘neither agree nor disagree’ responses (29.7%) warns against inferring patterns of widespread hostility, this does suggest open affirmation and recognition of worldviews represented in the RE classroom is variable and selective. Nevertheless, the fact ‘agree’ responses make up a majority of responses for each statement suggests the worldviews style of RE has become – or at least is becoming – normative across schools in England and Wales. This may indicate a deliberate adoption of a worldviews approach to RE curricula by a teacher, or the presence of associated assumptions in the class experience as a consequence of ‘worldviews’ language resonating with wider cultural norms. The disparate and partial adoption of worldviews RE across the sector suggests a combination of the two is most likely.

Statistically significant results from the subsequent chi-square tests of association revealed notable patterns of engagement with a worldviews approach across several variables. First, students who attended secondary schools with a religious character were more likely to feel engaged in classroom discussions than those who attended schools without a religious character. But they were also more likely to feel excluded in other ways. They were more likely than their peers in non-religious schools to report that they had talked about their own worldview in class (60.3% vs. 48.1%) and that they had learnt about the complexity of both religious and non-religious perspectives (73.9% vs. 63.2%). Yet they were also more likely to report _disagreement_ that their worldviews were respected (21.8% vs. 10.7%) and that they had studied alongside classmates with diverse beliefs (27.3% vs. 22.6%). They were also more likely to disagree that worldviews can be shaped by personal decisions as well as tradition (12.1% vs. 9.2%).

Second, the stage of study influenced experiences. Students who had studied RE at AS or A Level reported higher levels of agreement with the statements than those who only studied RE until GCSE or Year 9. They were more likely to say they studied alongside classmates with a range of worldviews (73% vs. 59.6% GCSE and 54.5% Year 9), to have talked about their own worldview in the RE classroom (57.9% vs. 51.4% and 44.6%), and to feel that their personal perspectives were respected (66.7% vs. 55% and 51.7%). These findings suggest that longer and more advanced engagement with RE is associated with richer classroom experiences, rather than just greater factual knowledge.

Lastly, religious identity was statistically significant. Both Christian and minority religious students reported greater engagement in a worldviews approach than non-religious students. A clear majority of minority religious students (79.3%) and Christians (61.3%) reported that they studied alongside classmates with a range of religious and non-religious worldviews, compared with 56.1% of non-religious students. Similarly, 71.3% of minority religious students and 51.8% of Christian students reported talking about their own worldview in class, compared with 47% of non-religious students. Feelings of respect followed the same pattern: 74% of minority religious students and 57% of Christians felt their worldviews were respected, compared with 55.9% of non-religious students. This pattern suggests that the RE classroom can be a more affirming and validating place for religious students, perhaps because the subject matter as currently framed resonates more closely with their lived experiences, or the opportunities to share and have their perspectives respected offer a sense of visibility missing elsewhere in school. By contrast, lower levels of engagement among non-religious students highlight a potential imbalance in the way that RE is currently framed, one that risks reinforcing the voices of religious students to the exclusion of others.

### The relationship between worldview engagement and ‘interfaith readiness’

We then asked, how, and to what extent, does a Religion and Worldviews approach prepare students for the challenges of relating to others different from themselves at university? Table 5 provides the results of the OLS regression analyses exploring the relationship between students’ engagement in worldviews in the RE classroom and their baseline measure of pluralism (including the ‘overall pluralism orientation’ variable, alongside the four sub-scales) upon enrolling in their undergraduate studies at university.

### Table 5.  OLS regressions indicating the relationship between worldviews-related engagement in the RE classroom and students’ baseline measures of pluralism upon enrolment at university (_N_ = 824–825).

[Download CSV](https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0005&doi=10.1080%2F01416200.2026.2706090&downloadType=CSV)Display Table

The most consistently and strongly significant predictor of pluralism was students’ worldviews learning outcomes, reinforcing the notion that _what_ students learn in RE remains key. Students who reported learning in RE that worldviews can be religious or non-religious, that both religious and non-religious worldviews are shaped not only by tradition but by personal decisions, that such worldviews are internally complex, and that there is diversity within religious and non-religious traditions demonstrated higher levels of all of our measures of pluralism upon enrolment to university. While we cannot directly infer causality, this pattern suggests that worldviews-related content, whether intentionally taught or not, may be particularly influential, lending empirical support to CoRE’s 2018 call for a substantive and formalised curricular shift towards RE teaching that foregrounds the diversity, complexity, and lived nature of both religious and non-religious worldviews. Moreover, in response to the 2025 Curriculum Review’s claim that ‘RE in many schools is not good enough and does not prepare pupils adequately for life beyond school’ (Gov.uk Citation 2025, 108), these findings help to specify _what kinds of learning_ within RE may best contribute to students’ readiness to engage in post-school environments characterised by diverse worldview communities. Namely, reforms grounded in a worldviews approach are likely to support precisely this.

Alongside learning outcomes, the perception of diversity within the RE classroom consistently predicted students’ pluralism upon entering university, with the exception of global citizenship. In other words, students who perceived their school RE classrooms as spaces where a range of religious and non-religious worldviews were represented were more likely to demonstrate readiness to engage across worldview differences at university. This finding resonates with previous research linking perceived diversity to pluralistic attitudes (Bowman Citation 2012; Aune et al. Citation 2025), suggesting that learning RE within a context of assumed difference, where diversity is expected, rather than exceptional, positively shapes students’ preparedness for diversity in non-classroom contexts.

A more puzzling finding concerns the negative relationship between feeling that one’s own worldview is respected in the RE classroom and outcomes related to global citizenship. Whilst this finding appears counterintuitive, and in opposition to previous work that links insensitivity to decreases in interfaith learning (Aune et al. Citation 2025; Rockenbach et al. Citation 2015) other work suggests that experiences of perceived insensitivity may prompt reflective learning and deeper engagement with difference (Peacock and Riggers-Piehl Citation 2025). Ultimately, we must interpret this finding with caution. It is inappropriate to conclude that diminished respect or insensitivity should be used as a pedagogical strategy in RE. Instead, the challenge is to identify alternative ways of creating constructive encounters that stretch students to engage with difference – a concept we call ‘provocative encounters’ in other analyses (Aune et al. Citation 2025; Fryer et al. Citation 2026) – while ensuring that respect and inclusion remain core principles of RE.

## Conclusion, limitations and implications

We sought to answer two questions: 1. What aspects of a Religion and Worldviews approach do first-year UK university undergraduates recall experiencing in the school RE classroom? and 2. How, if at all, does a Religion and Worldviews approach prepare students for the challenges of relating to others different from themselves once they are at university?

In response to our first question, we found that while the concept of worldviews appears increasingly embedded in what is taught in the RE classroom, reports of discussion of one’s own personal worldviews, and the perception among students that personal worldviews are respected, are less consistent. Engagement varies by school type, stage of study, and religious identity, suggesting that whilst a worldviews approach to RE may be becoming normative in terms of content, it remains uneven in practice.

Responding to our second question, our analysis revealed strong positive relationships between worldview-related learning outcomes (for example, learning about the complex nature and internal diversity of religious and non-religious worldviews), and students’ ‘interfaith readiness’ on entry to university. Perceived worldview diversity within the RE classroom is also significant, highlighting the benefits of learning in contexts of assumed difference.

We acknowledge several limitations when interpreting these findings. Across our five regression models, R 2 values ranged from .110 to .242, indicating that the RE experiences accounted for between 11% and 24.2% of the variance in students’ pluralism on entry to university. This means that, as we might reasonably expect, a substantial proportion of variance is explained by other factors, such as personal characteristics, school-level influences, and wider social contexts. Moreover, our sample size precluded a multilevel modelling approach, which would have generated a more nuanced examination of the interaction between individual- and school-level variables. Future research drawing on a larger sample would increase statistical power and allow for this modelling.

Our findings present other avenues for future research, including that which explores the consequences of talking about personal worldviews and feeling that one’s worldview is respected; these are the aspects of the RE classroom fewest students reported experiencing, and their relationship with students’ ‘interfaith readiness’ is unclear. Moreover, pluralism orientation is but one aspect of ‘interfaith readiness’. We might reasonably expect that the independent variables might interact differently with the other two outcomes used in the Interfaith Learning and Development conceptual framework: ‘self authored worldview commitment (reflexively constructing personal worldviews in dialogue with those that are different) and appreciative attitudes towards named religious groups different from one’s own (Mayhew and Rockenbach Citation 2021). Research that explores the role of RE in students’ interfaith learning development across all three domains would be beneficial.

We suggest that adapting RE to reflect a plurality of religious and non-religious worldview orientations is not just a matter of representation or inclusion, but one that has meaningful educational and social consequences for students when they leave school. As such, we draw implications from our findings for RE professionals. First, there is a need for RE teachers and curriculum or syllabus designers to ensure that non-religious perspectives are given appropriate weight alongside religious ones. This means not only teaching about secular and humanist perspectives, but encouraging non-religious students to articulate their views in a space that feels safe and respected.

Second, schools with a religious character should be more intentional about drawing on diverse perspectives, particularly non-religious ones, to ensure all students feel represented. Creating classroom spaces in which worldviews are explored beyond the dominant tradition could help balance opportunities for personal reflection with a stronger sense of belonging. These first two recommendations build on others’ work on non-religious students’ experiences of RE, such as Strhan and Shillitoe (Citation 2022), who argue that many non-religious pupils experience a ‘hermeneutic injustice’ (2022: 261) due to them ‘not being given meaningful opportunities to explore their own worldviews’ in the RE classroom (263).

Third, for schools situated in more religiously and culturally homogeneous areas, where it is difficult to assume diversity through classroom demographics alone, a range of religious and non-religious perspectives need to be intentionally integrated into curriculum content and pedagogy. We recognise this as a balancing act; whilst teachers must acknowledge and affirm the diversity that is present in the pupil body, they must also recognise where diversity is absent, avoiding framing diverse perspectives in ways that feel remote or abstract. Casson et al. (Citation 2023) study of the rural church primary school illustrates this. They emphasise the need for ‘attention to the context of each rural parish, and community’, recognising that rural school communities may draw pupils from dispersed catchment areas and that connections are often ‘brittle and fragile’ (2023: 105). Effective practice therefore needs careful pedagogical reflection on how difference is constructed and/or foregrounded in order to support students in engaging with perspectives that are not explicitly represented in their peer group.

Lastly, our key finding from the regression analyses, that worldview-related learning outcomes are associated with greater pluralism upon starting university, raises important implications for assessment. If outcomes framed in this analysis, such as understanding the internal complexity of religious and non-religious worldviews, or recognising the role of personal decision-making in worldview formation, are educationally consequential, then existing models of assessment may well be insufficient. Whilst specific recommendations for assessment fall outside the remit of this paper, we would endorse a framework that captures interpretive and reflexive forms of learning. Emerging models of religious literacy that foreground worldview complexity, positionality, and encounter with plurality, such as Shaw’s concept of ‘worldview literacy’ (Shaw Citation 2022), may offer a productive starting point for rethinking how learning in RE is conceptualised and measured.

## Notes

1. Enrolments in the 2023/24 academic year totalled 2,904,425 (Higher Education Statistics Agency Citation 2025a).

2. In the 2023/24 academic year, 732,285 international students enrolled, 25.2% of the overall student population. This represents a rise of 32% increase on the 554,375 international student enrolments in 2019/20 (Higher Education Statistics Agency Citation 2025b).

3. While the sample includes students educated in both England and Wales, it is important to note that the formal implementation of a Religion and Worldviews approach was still emerging across both contexts during the period when participants were in secondary education. In Wales, this coincided with the 2022 development of RE as ‘Religion, Values and Ethics’, while in England the adoption of Religion and Worldviews-informed syllabi and curricula also developed gradually following the Commission on Religious Education’s (Citation 2018) report. Consequently, we do not assume that participants were taught through a formally designated Religion and Worldviews curriculum. Rather, our measures capture students’ reported experiences of pedagogical and curricular features commonly associated with a Religion and Worldviews approach, including engagement with religious and non-religious worldviews, worldview diversity, and the complexity and internal diversity of traditions.

4. Note, of those who did attend a secondary school with a religious character, 198 students provided information on their school’s denominational ethos. 85% attended Christian schools (48.3% Roman Catholic and 36.7% Church of England). The remaining students attended Hindu, Jewish, Muslim or Sikh schools, or those with an ‘other’ denominational affiliation. Due to the small sample size of students from secondary schools with religious characters, we were unable to conduct analysis at the level of individual denomination.

5. All chi-square findings reported in this article are significant at the _p_< 0.05 level or below.

6. For all of the regression analyses variables, we only consider a measure reliable if its Cronbach’s alpha (a) statistic reached approximately .70 or higher (see Matsunaga Citation 2010).

# 2022 Report on International Religious Freedom: Nigeria

##### [Download Report](https://www.state.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/441219-NIGERIA-2022-INTERNATIONAL-RELIGIOUS-FREEDOM-REPORT.pdf)
